en: Preface to the Publication of the *Haedong-sō* (Sea-East Commentary) on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Regarding commentaries on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, there have been three types throughout antiquity: those by Fazang, Huìyuǎn, and Wŏnhyo.
These are known in the world as the "Three Masters of the Root Treatise. Among these, the first two commentaries were circulated in the world for many years.
This is indeed ancient. It is simply that the karmic conditions for it have only now ripened.
As for this commentary (*śāstra*), we have heard that its original manuscript exists, yet no one has read it for many years; thus, the time was simply not yet ripe.

Regarding what is called the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*), Master Qingliang Guanding states in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (received by him from Fazang in Huainan): "This work stands far above those of all other masters."
The "Superior" [version] is that which should be known. Although I have frequently cited it within the chapters of my own treatise, I have not seen its complete commentary.
For this reason, I have been remiss in investigating the beginning and end of that commentary; consequently, my fellow students who carry their satchels cannot help but feel a sense of regret.
Recently, a certain Mr. Yin told me that someone had presented him with a copy of this brocade-bound edition. It is...
I have permitted this to be carved into woodblocks for circulation and pray that you will deign to examine and correct it; your words are most earnest.

Furthermore, I reflected that the time and conditions were now just right, and I rejoiced at the arrival of this commentary. Having nodded my head in agreement to accept it, I have taken it up to read and collate it.

Nevertheless, as my natural endowment is as sluggish as a hack, I am unable to exhaust my full strength; how could I dare to engage in profound contemplation? I humbly entreat the great masters to favor me with their governance of this work.
Recorded respectfully by Kakugen at Chikaku-mon in Higashiyama, Kyoto,
on an autumn day in the year of Kyōroku 9, the *Hinoe-ushi* (1696),
for Volume One of the Combined Edition of the Commentary and Notes on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Liang Dynasty;
with commentary by the Sramana Yuanxiao of Haedong during the Tang Dynasty (including separate notes).
In explaining this treatise, there are briefly three sections: first, the indication of the essential nature; second, the explanation of the title;
and third, the elucidation of the meaning based on the text.
Regarding the first, the indication of the essential nature: as for the essence of the Mahāyāna, it is ethereally empty and tranquil, profoundly still...
How profound and mysterious it is! That which is "mysterious beyond the mysterious" surely does not transcend the realm of the myriad phenomena.
That which is "quiescent beyond the quiescent" still remains within the discourses of the hundred schools. It is not merely beyond form; even the five eyes cannot perceive its body.
It is not merely within words; even the four types of eloquence cannot describe its appearance. If one wishes to call it "great," it enters the innermost void without leaving anything behind.
The desire to speak is subtle; it encompasses all without exteriority yet remains inexhaustible. When drawn toward existence, it is as if one were using emptiness;
when attained within non-existence, the myriad things ride upon it to be born. Not knowing how to describe it, we have forcibly designated it as the Mahāyāna.
(Explanatory Note) As for its essence: it is vast, like the great void, yet devoid of self-interest. It is expansive, like the immense ocean, yet possesses supreme impartiality.
Because it possesses supreme impartiality, movement and stillness are spontaneously established. Because it is devoid of self-interest, defilement and purity are thus harmonized.
Because defilement and purity are harmonized, the ultimate and the conventional are equal. Because movement and stillness are established, [the two truths are realized].

Ascending and descending differ; because ascending and descending differ, the path of resonance and response is opened. Because the ultimate and the conventional are equal, the path of conceptual thought is severed.
Because conceptual thought is severed, those who realize this body ride upon shadows and echoes without fixed direction, for resonance and response are pervasive.
Those who pray transcend names and forms yet find a place of return. These bestowed shadows and echoes are neither form nor speech.

Having already transcended names and signs, what is there to transcend and what is there to return to? This is called the ultimate principle where no principle exists, the great "so-it-is" where nothing is so.
Were it not for the Great Being who has sealed his mouth and the Man of Integrity who perceives through direct observation, who could discourse upon the Mahāyāna beyond words? It arises...

How can one have deep faith in those who have transcended all conceptual thought? For this reason, Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, through his unconditioned great compassion, lamented that the ocean of the mind is easily tossed about by the delusive winds of ignorance;
and he took pity on this true nature of original enlightenment, which is difficult to awaken to while one sleeps in the long dream of saṃsāra.
Thus, with the power of wisdom that realizes the identity of self and others, he was capable of composing this treatise to praise and expound upon the profound sūtras of the Tathāgata.
This profound meaning intends to allow students to briefly open a single scroll to thoroughly explore the purport of the Tripiṭaka,
and to enable those who seek the Way to forever find rest within the myriad realms and thereby return to the source of the One Mind.
(Additional Note) As for their treatises, there is nothing they do not establish and nothing they do not refute.

Like the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and others, they universally refute all attachments and even refute the refutations themselves, yet they do not concede to the existence of either the refuter or the refuted.
This is called the "treatise that goes forth but does not return. Such are the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and other works.
He establishes a general framework of profound and shallow levels to categorize the various Dharma gates, yet he does not rigidly adhere to or discard the systems he himself has formulated;
this is what is called "giving without taking away. Now, this commentator is both wise and benevolent, as well as profound and broad in learning.
There is nothing that is not established and then spontaneously discarded, and nothing that is not refuted and then subsequently affirmed.

As for "subsequently affirming," this reveals that the former [position] has reached its ultimate limit and is universally established. As for "spontaneously discarding," this clarifies that the latter [position], having exhausted its giving, is now taken away.
This is called the progenitor of all treatises and the arbiter of all disputes.

Although what has been described is extensive, it may be summarized as follows: By opening two gates within the single mind, the broad teachings of the one hundred and eight *māras* are comprehensively encompassed;
by revealing the purity of nature amidst the defilement of phenomena, the profound subtleties of the fifteen *yūja* are universally integrated.
Such as the single flavor of the Hamsa Grove; the non-dual intent of Vulture Peak; the ultimate fruit of the three bodies with the same nature as the Golden Drum;
the profound causes of the four stages in the *Avataṃsaka* and *Ratnakūṭa*; the vast and expansive supreme path of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* and *Mahāsaṃnipāta*;
and the subtle and esoteric gateways of the *Sūryagarbha* and *Candragarbha*—all such scriptures among the multitude of the canon.
This is the very core of my liver and heart. That which penetrates it all as one—could it be anything other than this treatise? Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"Because one wishes to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast, profound, and extensive Dharma, one should expound this treatise.
Since the intent of this treatise is thus, when expanded, its primary thesis consists of immeasurable and boundless meanings; when condensed, it comprises two gates.
The Dharma of the single mind is the essential core. Within these two gates, ten thousand meanings are contained without confusion;
boundless meanings are unified and harmoniously fused within the single mind. Therefore, opening and closing are sovereign, and establishing and refuting are unimpeded.
One may open without becoming prolix, and close without becoming narrow; one may establish without gain, and refute without loss. This is the [teaching] of Aśvaghoṣa.

This *Miaoshu* (Exquisite Commentary) is the very essence of the school that gives rise to faith. However, because the purport of this treatise is profound and deep, those who have hitherto interpreted it have rarely grasped its core tenets.
This is truly because each person clings to their own habitual learning and is led by the literal text, unable to maintain an open mind in seeking its ultimate meaning;
thus, they do not approach the intent of the Master of the Treatise. Some look toward the source and lose the current, while others grasp the leaves.
Yet the core has perished; some have cut away the collar to patch the sleeves, while others have broken off the branches to bring back the roots.

Now, I shall simply rely on this treatise as it corresponds to the scriptural text under discussion, so that those who share the same goal may adjust their understanding accordingly. The delineation of the fundamental principle and its essence is concluded.
Next, the title shall be explained. Regarding the term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle): "Great" (*mahā*) is the name of the Dharma itself, with the meaning of being vast and all-encompassing.
"Vehicle" (*yāna*) is a metaphorical designation, with the function of transporting and carrying. Although this is the general explanation, when analyzed therein, there are two approaches:
first, according to the sūtras; second, according to the śāstras. As for the explanation according to the sūtras, it is as in the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: "The Mahāyāna is so called because it is immeasurable, boundless, and limitless; because it pervades all things like space;
because it is vast and accommodates all sentient beings; and because it is not shared with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—it is therefore named the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, as for the 'vehicle' (yāna): it takes the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as its wheels, and with goodness..."
The ten pure wholesome karmas serve as the spokes; the accumulation of pure merit serves as the hub;
firm, ultimate, and single-minded concentration serves as the linchpins, axle-nuts, nails, and wedges; the successful accomplishment of the various dhyānas and liberations serves as the shafts;
the four immeasurables serve as the excellent harnessing; and spiritual friends serve as the charioteer; while knowing the proper and improper times serves as the departure.
It moves, driven by the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; it is harnessed with the reins of the seven jewels of awakening;
it is girthed with the straps of the five pure eyes; and it displays the streamers and banners of vast, upright, and universal great compassion.
Taking the four right efforts as the linchpins (the wooden pins that secure the axle), taking the four foundations of mindfulness as the level and straight alignment,
taking the four bases of psychic power as the swift advance, taking the five superior powers as the inspection of the battlefield, taking the eightfold noble path as the direct course,
and taking the unobstructed wisdom-illumination regarding all sentient beings as the carriage frame, one turns back the six perfections through non-abiding.

It is directed toward *samyak-saṃbodhi* (perfect enlightenment) and, by means of the four unobstructed truths, it carries one across to the other shore; this is the Mahāyāna. The commentary explains: "The preceding twenty phrases have employed metaphors to illustrate the Dharma and thereby reveal the meaning of the vehicle. Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "This vehicle is that which is received by all Buddhas, observed by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and mounted by all Bodhisattvas. Explanation: The term "vehicle" (*yāna*) is used here as a metaphor for the path. It signifies that which carries sentient beings from the state of suffering to the state of bliss, and from the state of birth and death to the state of Nirvāṇa. This is why it is called the "Mahāyāna," the Great Vehicle. Regarding the phrase "four unobstructed truths": the four truths are the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. They are called "unobstructed" because they are free from the three obstacles—namely, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstacle of knowable objects (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). Because these four truths are free from these three obstacles, they are termed "unobstructed. By means of these four unobstructed truths, one crosses over to the other shore, which is the state of perfect enlightenment. This is the Mahāyāna. As for the passage "this vehicle is that which is received by all Buddhas": "received" means that the Buddhas have attained it. "Observed by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" means that while they have not yet fully realized it, they nevertheless contemplate it. "Mounted by all Bodhisattvas" means that they ride upon it to proceed toward the state of Buddhahood. Thus, it is known that the Mahāyāna is the most supreme among all vehicles. It is the ultimate path traversed by all sages. Therefore, it is called the Great Vehicle. It is also called the "Vehicle of the Bodhisattva" because it is the path mounted by those seeking to attain perfect enlightenment. It is also called the "Vehicle of the Buddha" because it is the path through which all Buddhas have emerged. It is also called the "Vehicle of Liberation" because it can deliver sentient beings from the bonds of birth and death. It is also called the "Vehicle of the Dharma" because it is the path that manifests the true reality of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Wisdom" because it is the path that realizes the wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing. It is also called the "Vehicle of Compassion" because it is the path that universally delivers all sentient beings. It is also called the "Vehicle of Merit" because it is the path that accumulates immeasurable merit. It is also called the "Vehicle of Expedient Means" because it is the path that employs various skillful methods to guide sentient beings. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-duality" because it is the path that transcends all dualistic views. It is also called the "Vehicle of Emptiness" because it is the path that realizes the nature of emptiness of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Signlessness" because it is the path that is free from all signs and characteristics. It is also called the "Vehicle of Wishlessness" because it is the path that is free from all desires and attachments. It is also called the "Vehicle of No-Abode" because it is the path that has no fixed dwelling place. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-action" because it is the path that is free from all conceptual constructions and mental activities. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-discrimination" because it is the path that is free from all false discrimination. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-attachment" because it is the path that is free from all attachments and clingings. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-obstruction" because it is the path that is free from all obstacles and hindrances. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-retrogression" because it is the path from which there is no turning back. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-extinction" because it is the path that is eternal and inexhaustible. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-birth" because it is the path that is free from the cycle of birth and death. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-death" because it is the path that is free from the fear of death. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-suffering" because it is the path that is free from all suffering and distress. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-bliss" because it is the path that transcends the duality of pleasure and pain. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-self" because it is the path that realizes the non-existence of a self. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-dharma" because it is the path that realizes the non-existence of phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-duality" because it is the path that transcends the duality of existence and non-existence. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-conceptualization" because it is the path that is free from all conceptualizations and discursive thoughts. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-manifestation" because it is the path that does not manifest any forms or appearances. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-perception" because it is the path that is free from all perceptions and cognitions. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-grasping" because it is the path that is free from all grasping and seizing. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-rejection" because it is the path that does not reject or discard anything. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-coming" because it is the path that has no point of arrival. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-going" because it is the path that has no point of departure. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-abiding" because it is the path that does not abide anywhere. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-resting" because it is the path that does not rest in any state. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-movement" because it is the path that is free from all movement and agitation. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-stillness" because it is the path that is free from all stillness and stagnation. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-arising" because it is the path that is free from all arising and production. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-ceasing" because it is the path that is free from all ceasing and destruction. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-birth" because it is the path that is free from the birth of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-death" because it is the path that is free from the death of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-suffering" because it is the path that is free from the suffering of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-bliss" because it is the path that is free from the bliss of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-self" because it is the path that is free from the self of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-dharma" because it is the path that is free from the dharmas of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-duality" because it is the path that is free from the duality of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-conceptualization" because it is the path that is free from the conceptualization of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-manifestation" because it is the path that is free from the manifestation of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-perception" because it is the path that is free from the perception of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-grasping" because it is the path that is free from the grasping of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-rejection" because it is the path that is free from the rejection of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-coming" because it is the path that is free from the coming of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-going" because it is the path that is free from the going of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-abiding" because it is the path that is free from the abiding of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-resting" because it is the path that is free from the resting of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-movement" because it is the path that is free from the movement of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-stillness" because it is the path that is free from the stillness of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-arising" because it is the path that is free from the arising of all phenomena. It is also called the "Vehicle of Non-ceasing" because it is the path that is free from the ceasing of
He is one whom Brahmā and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) should revere; he is one whom all sentient beings should honor; he is one whom all the wise should praise;
he is one to whom all the world should turn for refuge; he cannot be destroyed by any Māras;
he cannot be fathomed by any non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); and no one in the entire world can rival him. The commentary explains:
The preceding ten phrases have clarified the Mahāyāna in relation to persons. According to the treatise (*śāstra*), there are seven [types] and three [types].
The three kinds of great significance will be explained below. Regarding the "seven kinds," there are two sets of seven.
The first is as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*: "It is called the Mahāyāna because it is endowed with seven kinds of greatness. What are they?

Seventh, the greatness of the object (*ālambana-mahattva*): because the path of the bodhisattva takes as its object the vast teachings of immeasurable sūtras, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and so forth.
Second, the greatness of the practice (*pratipatti-mahattva*): because one correctly practices all the vast deeds for the benefit of oneself and others.
Third, the greatness of wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*): because one thoroughly understands the great selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Fourth is the greatness of diligence, because for three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one diligently cultivates immeasurable difficult practices through skillful means.
Fifth is the greatness of skill in means (*upāya-kauśalya*), because one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Sixth is the greatness of realization (*prāpti-mahattva*), because one attains the immeasurable and innumerable great qualities of the Tathāgata, such as the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

Seventh is the greatness of activity (*karma-mahattva*), because until the end of saṃsāra, one manifests all the vast deeds of a Buddha, such as the demonstration of attaining enlightenment (*bodhi*). (Among these, the first five are causes and the latter two are results. Second:
The *Xianyang lun* states: "The nature of the Mahāyāna refers to the Bodhisattvayāna being conjoined with seven kinds of greatness;

therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna. What are these seven? First is the greatness of the Dharma (*dharmamahātmya*), which refers to the vast teachings of skillful means contained within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka among the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Second is the greatness of the resolve (*cittotpādamahātmya*), which refers to that which has already been generated..."

1. The mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*). 2. The greatness of superior resolve (*adhimukti-mahattva*): that is, giving rise to superior faith and resolve regarding the aforementioned objects of the greatness of the Dharma.

3. The greatness of intention (*āśaya-mahattva*): that is, having already transcended the stage of practice through resolve (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one enters the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*).
4. The greatness of the provisions (*saṃbhāra-mahattva*): the accomplishment of the two great provisions of merit and wisdom.
Therefore, one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Sixth is the greatness of time, which refers to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment over the course of three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Seventh is the greatness of fulfillment, which refers to the very essence of the fulfillment that constitutes the body of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; compared to other forms of fulfilled essence, it is supreme.
Its essence is such that there is nothing equal to it, let alone anything superior. Both the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* speak in this same way.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In this context, whether it be the greatness of the dharma, or even the greatness of time—these six kinds are all causes for the great nature of perfect realization.
The great nature of perfect realization is the fruit of these preceding six kinds of greatness."
The commentary states: Although these two types of sevenfold greatness are identical in number, their intended purpose for establishment differs.
That intended purpose can be understood by investigating it. The explanation of the *Mahāyāna* is now complete. Regarding the term "arousing faith," it is based on this treatise.
It gives rise to faith in sentient beings; therefore, it is called "giving rise to faith.

Faith is defined by the expression of certainty—that is, the conviction that the principle truly exists, that cultivation can attain it, and that when attained through cultivation, there are infinite virtues.

Among these, the conviction that [the principle] truly exists constitutes the greatness of the essence of faith, because it is the conviction that all phenomena are unattainable; this is precisely what it means to believe in true existence.

Regarding the phrase "the dharma-realm as it truly is": that which can be attained through faith is the greatness of the aspect of faith (*śraddhā-nimitta-mahatva*), because it possesses the merit of its nature and perfumes sentient beings;

thus, being perfumed by the aspect of faith, one will inevitably return to the source. That which possesses inexhaustible meritorious functions is the greatness of the function of faith (*śraddhā-karma-mahatva*), for there is nothing it does not accomplish.
If a person can give rise to these three types of faith, they will be able to enter the Buddha-dharma and be born therein.
All merits emerge from the realms of Māra and reach the Unsurpassed Way. As a verse in a sutra says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of all merits;
it increases all roots of goodness, eliminates all doubts and delusions, and reveals and opens up the Unsurpassed Way.
Faith is able to transcend the realms of all Māras and reveal the unsurpassed path of liberation."
The indestructible seed of all merit gives birth to the tree of unsurpassed bodhi.
Because one relies on this treatise to give rise to the mind [of awakening], knowing that such immeasurable merit exists, it is said that "faith is aroused.

As for what is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*), it refers to words and phrases that establish, resolve, and provide a standard for practice, which definitively explain the principles of the profound characteristics of phenomena. Based on these definitive and decisive meanings, it is so named.
To summarize: the Mahāyāna is the fundamental essence of this treatise, while the *Awakening of Faith* is its preeminent capacity.
By presenting both essence and function together, the title is established; thus, it is called the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
△ Third, the explanation of the text. The text consists of three parts: the first three stanzas consist of the homage, salutation, and statement of intent;
the section beginning with "The Treatise says" below establishes the body of the treatise; and the final stanza summarizes and dedicates the merit.
△ Within the first three verses, there are two intended meanings. The first two stanzas correctly take refuge in the Triple Gem;
the final stanza describes the purpose for composing this treatise.
I take refuge in those who pervade the entirety of the ten directions, The most supreme ones, the all-knowing, The World-Saviors of unimpeded mastery over form,
And the Great Compassionate Ones, As well as their physical marks and signs, The ocean of true suchness of the nature of phenomena,
The treasury of immeasurable merit, And those who practice in accordance with reality.

In the opening expression of homage, there are two parts. The two characters "take refuge" (*namas*) constitute the aspect of the one who takes refuge. The passage beginning with "Throughout the ten directions" reveals the virtues of the object of refuge.
Regarding the aspect of the one who takes refuge: the meaning of "reverence and compliance" is the meaning of "taking refuge," and the meaning of "tending toward" is the meaning of "taking refuge."
"Life" (*jīva*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). It governs all the sense faculties and is the essential core of the single body;

life alone is the sovereign, that which all living beings value most, and nothing precedes it. To offer up this peerless life to serve the Unsurpassed Honored One expresses the ultimate limit of faith;
therefore, one speaks of "taking refuge in life" (*namas*). Furthermore, "taking refuge" has the meaning of returning to the source. Why is this so? Because sentient beings...
The six sense organs arise from the one mind, yet they turn their backs on their own source and scatter toward the six objects of sensory dust.
Now, by offering up one's life, one collectively gathers the six emotions and returns them to their origin, the source of the one mind; therefore, it is called "taking refuge" (*namas*).

That which is taken as refuge—the one mind—is itself the Triple Gem. From the words "Throughout the ten directions" below, the virtues of that which is taken as refuge are revealed; herein, the Triple Gem should be explained.
The meaning [of this] is as explained elsewhere. For now, we shall analyze the text. Within the text there are three parts, namely: Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Within these Jewels, there are also three intended meanings: first, praising the virtue of the mind; second, praising the virtue of form; and third, citing the person to conclude the praise.
Within the praise of the virtue of the mind, both its function and essence are praised. The initial statement, "the most supreme activity throughout the ten directions," praises its function.

This praises the function of his activity; that is to say, the activity of manifesting the eight signs and so forth to transform sentient beings throughout the entirety of the ten directions and across the limits of the three periods of time, performing all Buddha-works according to those who can be transformed. Therefore, it is said: "the most supreme activity throughout the ten directions."

As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: "The greatness of karma consists in its persistence until the end of saṃsāra, manifesting the attainment of enlightenment and so forth for all beings, and establishing the vast activities of the Buddhas.
While that passage refers to the three periods of time, this one reveals the ten directions.
The term "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) praises the essence of wisdom. The reason its activity pervades the ten directions is that the essence of wisdom is all-pervasive.
Because the essence of wisdom is omnipresent, it is called "omniscient. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Just as space pervades the limits of all forms, yet is without arising, abiding, ceasing, or transformation, so too is the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
It is likewise so. Because it is unerring and immutable throughout all that is knowable, the praise of the qualities of the mind is concluded.

Next is the praise of the qualities of form (*rūpa*). Within this, there are also two parts. "Form is unimpeded" praises the excellence of the essence of form; "sovereignty" praises the superiority of the function of form.
Regarding the first, the "essence of form," it refers to the Tathāgata’s form-body (*rūpakāya*), which is accomplished through the myriad practices and is inconceivable.

It is discussed as being accomplished through habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*). Although it possesses wondrous form, it is without obstruction. Its single mark and single excellence are boundless and limitless;
therefore, it is said that it guides form without hindrance. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"One might still be able to find the limit of space, but there is no shore or limit to a single pore of the Buddha. The virtues of the Buddha are thus inconceivable; this is called the Tathāgata."

Because their knowledge and vision are pure, although they lack substantiality and obstruction, there is the principle of manifestation within spatial dimensions; thus, they are termed "form" (rūpa) while remaining unobstructed.
As for the term "mastery" (vaśitā), it praises the function of form, meaning that the five sense organs function interchangeably and the ten bodies act in concert with one another;
therefore, it is said that "form is mastered. Regarding the interchangeability of the five sense organs, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle eight:

This is explained within the context of mastery (*vaśitā*). Regarding the "one who performs the marks of the ten bodies," this is as described in the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Having concluded the praise of his physical excellence, the phrase "the Great Compassionate Savior of the World" constitutes the third line, which identifies the person and summarizes the praise.

The Buddha is like a great elder who regards sentient beings as his children; entering the burning house of the triple world (*tridhātu*), he rescues them from the suffering of being consumed by fire. Therefore, it is said:
"World-Savior. The virtue of being a World-Savior is precisely Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). It is compassion that transcends [the distinction between] self and other;

it is objectless compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*), the most excellent among all forms of compassion, and is therefore called "Great Compassion. Among the ten thousand virtues possessed within the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), the Tathāgata employs Great Compassion alone as his power;
thus, it is singled out to manifest the person of the Buddha. As the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In general..."
The power of the noble ones is of six kinds. What are these six? Infants have crying as their power;
when they wish to say something, they must first cry. Women have anger as their power; it is only after relying upon anger that they speak.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have patience as their power; they always maintain a humble mind toward others before speaking for themselves.
"Chen. The king takes pride and arrogance as his power, and by means of this haughty authority, he proclaims himself.

Arhats take single-minded diligence as their power, and they proclaim themselves. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, take great compassion as their power, for the sake of extensively benefiting sentient beings.
Thus we know that the Buddhas uniquely take great compassion as their power; therefore, it is used here to indicate the person's name.
Regarding "the Great Compassionate One": the three preceding phrases have completed the praise of the Buddha Jewel. The following two phrases next reveal the Dharma Jewel.
As for "the essence and characteristics of that body," this refers to the body of the Tathāgata previously mentioned, which is the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body).
Since it takes the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as its very essence, it is called "the essence and characteristics of that body. This is the presentation of the Buddha.
One should take up this Dharma. The second phrase correctly reveals the essential nature and characteristics of the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).

Regarding the term "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*): it refers to *nirvāṇa*, the fundamental nature of all phenomena; thus, it is called "dharma-nature. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Dharma" means *nirvāṇa*, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
"Nature" (*tā*) means the original constituent essence, just as yellow stone has the nature of gold and white stone has the nature of silver. It is like this.
All phenomena possess the nature of nirvāṇa; therefore, they are called the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). Regarding the term "true thusness" (*tathatā*):
it is called "true" (*tathā*) because there is nothing to be discarded, and "thus" (*tathā*) because there is nothing to be established. As stated in the subsequent text:

"The essence of this true thusness has nothing that can be discarded, for all phenomena are entirely true. Nor is there anything that can be established, for all phenomena are identical to thusness. It should be understood accordingly.
Because all phenomena are known to be ineffable and inconceivable, they are called *tathatā* (suchness).

As for what is called the "ocean," it is used as a metaphor to manifest the Dharma; to speak of it briefly, the ocean has four meanings: first, its extreme depth; second, its vastness; third, its inexhaustible hundred treasures;
and fourth, the reflection of the myriad images within it. One should know that the great ocean of *tathatā* is likewise.
It is likewise so. Because it eternally severs the hundred negations; because it encompasses all phenomena; because there is no virtue it does not possess;
and because there is no form it does not manifest. Therefore, it is called the ocean of the *dharmatā-tathatā*. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"For example, like a deep great ocean, its precious treasures are inexhaustible, and within it are fully manifested the forms and images of all classes of sentient beings. It is profoundly deep.
The ocean of causes and conditions contains inexhaustible jewels of merit; for within the pure *dharmakāya*, there is no image that does not appear.
Having concluded the praise of the Jewel of the Dharma, the following two lines praise the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Regarding the phrase "the treasury of immeasurable merit":
To select individuals based on their virtues refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi). As they cultivate each single practice, the myriad practices are fully integrated;

each and every one of these practices is equal to the Dharma-realm and is without limit or measure. Because that which is attained through the accumulation of merit is thus immeasurable, it is called "immeasurable merit.
Such merit belongs entirely to the Bodhisattva; because a person can encompass these virtues, it is termed a "treasury" (kośa).
Next, regarding the phrase "practicing according to reality" (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*) and so forth, this is a formal praise of the virtue of practice.

According to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, it is termed "practice according to reality" in reference to the wisdom of the fundamental nature (*mūla-jñāna*), while the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is termed "universal practice.

Here, the mention of "practicing according to reality" cites the wisdom of the fundamental nature, while the subsequent mention of "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the subsequently attained wisdom. If one follows the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:

This teaching summarizes the beginning and end of all practices, which are collectively subsumed under two phrases: namely, practicing according to reality (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*) and non-negligence (*apramāda*).
As that sutra states: "Practicing according to reality" refers to generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*);
"non-negligence" refers to fulfilling the aspiration for enlightenment. Furthermore, "practicing according to reality" refers to the practice of giving (*dāna*).
Generosity. As for non-negligence, it means not seeking recompense. Thus maintaining pure ethical discipline, one achieves non-retrogression;

or practicing the conduct of patience, one attains the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Seeking all roots of goodness without weariness, one relinquishes all conditioned activities.
Cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not dwell in meditative concentration; fulfilling wisdom, one does not engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The Dharma, according to its sequence, consists of practicing in accordance with reality and non-negligence, and so forth, as explained at length.
Here, "practicing in accordance with reality" encompasses generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) up to the fulfillment of wisdom.
Next, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes non-negligence, which is the fulfillment of the aspiration for enlightenment up to the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
This is the Dharma. Having completed the homage to the Triple Gem,
it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to eliminate doubt, abandon false attachments, give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna,
and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
Next, the general purport of composing this treatise is set forth. This purport does not exceed two aspects:
the first half clarifies the purpose of transforming sentient beings below, while the second half reveals the purpose of propagating the Buddha-way above.

That sentient beings remain perpetually submerged in the ocean of birth and death and do not proceed toward the shore of nirvana is solely due to their doubts and perverse attachments; therefore, now...
This is the essential method for transforming sentient beings below: to cause them to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments. Generally speaking, there are many avenues of doubt;
however, for those seeking the Mahāyāna, there are two specific types of doubt. The first is doubt regarding the Dharma, which acts as an obstacle to the arousal of the bodhicitta.
The second is the gate of doubt, which obstructs spiritual practice. Regarding what is called "doubting the Dharma," it refers to raising this doubt:
"Is the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma one or many? If it were one, there would be no distinct dharmas; because there are no distinct dharmas, there would be no sentient beings.
For whom, then, would the Bodhisattva arouse his great vows? If it were many dharmas, then it would not be a single essence. If...
Because [sentient beings and the Buddha] are of one essence, yet objects and the self are each distinct, how can the Great Compassion of the same essence arise?
Due to this doubt, one is unable to resolve to practice. Regarding what is called the "gate of doubt": the teaching-gates established by the Tathāgata are numerous;

upon which gate should one rely to first initiate cultivation? If all gates may be relied upon together, one cannot enter them all at once. If one relies on only one or two, which ones should be set aside?

Why is this? Because due to these doubts, one is unable to initiate spiritual practice. Therefore, in order now to dispel these two kinds of doubt, we establish the doctrine of the single mind (*ekacitta-dharma*) and open two gates.
As for establishing the doctrine of the single mind: it dispels the former doubt by clarifying that the Mahāyāna Dharma consists solely of the single mind;
outside of the single mind, there are no other separate dharmas, though there is only the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).
From the single mind, various waves arise and circulate through the six realms. Although these waves of the six realms arise, they do not transcend the ocean of the single mind.
This is because the single mind moves and acts as the six realms; therefore, one is able to give rise to the vow for great salvation.

The six realms do not transcend the single mind; therefore, one is able to give rise to great compassion of identical substance (*sahaja-karuṇā*). By dispelling doubts in this manner, one attains the arousal of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

Regarding the opening of the two gates: this dispels the second doubt and clarifies that although there are many various teaching-gates, the initial entry into practice does not exceed these two gates.
One practices the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) by relying on the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and [one practices] by relying on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

One initiates contemplative practice through these gates, wherein calm abiding and insight are practiced in union; thus all myriad practices are fully prepared. By entering these two gates, one masters all other gates.
In this way, by dispelling doubt, one is able to initiate spiritual cultivation. Regarding the abandonment of false attachments, there are two types of false attachment.
What are called the attachment to persons (*pudgala-grāha*) and the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). The abandonment of these two meanings will be explained in the following text.
The preceding section concludes the transformation of sentient beings. The two lines below concern the upward propagation of the Buddha-way:

by eliminating doubts regarding those two extremes, one gives rise to resolute faith. Because one understands that the Mahāyāna is solely the One Mind, it is said that "one gives rise to the Great [Vehicle]."

This refers to riding upon right faith. By abandoning the two preceding attachments and conceptual discriminations, one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and is able to succeed to the rank of a Buddha;
thus it is said that "the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. As the treatise states:

"The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma—faith is that which enables entry, and wisdom is that which enables crossing. Therefore, by citing both faith and wisdom, it clarifies the propagation of the Buddha-way. [Verse]

The initial statement serves as the introduction, while the concluding phrase "therefore" indicates that this treatise was composed to clarify two specific intentions. This concludes the section on the homage and the statement of purpose.

From here follows the second part: the formal establishment of the body of the treatise. This section consists of three parts: first, the general heading and the promise to speak; second... [text continues]
The former [phrase] cites the number to introduce the chapter; the latter [phrase], "the three," provides a detailed explanation according to the sections of the text, as can be seen in the passage.
The treatise says: There exists a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained.

Regarding the statement at the beginning that there is "a dharma": this refers to the single dharma of the mind. If a person can understand this dharma, they will necessarily give rise to the vast faculty of faith;
therefore, it is said that they can give rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna. The characteristic of the faculty of faith is as explained in the title.
Once the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is established, one immediately enters the Buddha-way. Having entered the Buddha-way, one obtains inexhaustible treasures.
Such great benefits are attained by relying on this treatise; therefore, it should be explained. The general introduction and the promise to explain have already been concluded above.
The exposition consists of five divisions. What are these five? First, the Division on Causes and Conditions; second, the Division on Establishing the Thesis;
third, the Division on Exegesis; fourth, the Division on the Practice of Faith; and fifth, the Division on Encouraging Practice and its Benefits.

The second section provides the enumeration and opens the chapters. "There are five parts" indicates the number of chapters. The phrase "How so? and what follows below lists the titles of those chapters.
As for the "Section on Causes and Conditions," it is not without reason that the treatise begins here; it is the undertaking of the wise.

This must first be understood. Regarding the Section on Establishing the Thesis (*siddhānta-vibhāga*): since the causal conditions have already been set forth, it is appropriate to establish the correct thesis;

for if it were not briefly established, one would not know the essential tenets. Regarding the Section on Explanation (*vyākhyāna-vibhāga*): since the thesis has been briefly established, it should next be extensively analyzed.

If it were not explained and elucidated, its meaning and principles would be difficult to understand. As for the "Section on Cultivating Faith," since one relies upon this commentary to give rise to faith, one must certainly advance in practice;
for to have understanding without practice does not accord with the intent of the treatise. As for the "Section on the Benefits of Encouraging Practice":
Although the Dharma-gate of practicing with faith has been shown, those with meager roots of goodness are unwilling to cultivate it.
Therefore, its benefits are set forth to exhort them that they must certainly practice; hence, this is called the "Section on the Benefits of Exhorting Practice."
△ Below this is the third section, the detailed explanation according to the chapters, which consists of five parts.
△ Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the restatement of the chapter title; second, the manifestation of its causes and conditions.
First is the section on the exposition of causes and conditions (nidāna).
Within the manifestation of these causes and conditions, there are two question-and-answer sequences: the first is a direct exposition, and the second is the dispelling of doubts.
Question: By what causes and conditions was this treatise composed? Answer: There are eight kinds of such causes and conditions. What are they?
There are eight [reasons]. First, the general characteristic of the causal conditions:
namely, to cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and attain ultimate bliss, rather than seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Second, to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata, so that all sentient beings may achieve correct understanding without error. Third, to bring the roots of goodness to maturity.
First, because sentient beings are capable of not regressing in their faith regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma; second, to cause those sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate faith;

third, to demonstrate the skillful means for eliminating the obstacles of evil karma, to well-guard the mind, to remain far removed from delusion and pride, and to escape the net of error; fourth, to demonstrate the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote.

Because the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles have transcended [this state]; seventh, to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded mindfulness so that one may be born before the Buddha and never retreat from the faith;
and eighth, to demonstrate the benefits and encourage the practice of cultivation—for these and other such reasons, this treatise was composed.
The initial question is clear. In the response, there are three parts: a general introduction, a detailed explanation, and a concluding summary.

Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation, among the eight causal conditions, the first is the general characteristic cause (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-hetu*), and the latter seven are the specific characteristic causes (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-hetu*).
As for the first, the general characteristic, it has two meanings. First, whatever actions all bodhisattvas undertake, they always do so for the sake of the multitude...

The suffering of separation from birth is overcome and happiness is attained; this is not merely the cause for composing the treatise in this specific instance, and is therefore called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Second, although this cause serves as a condition for the section on the "Establishment of the Proposition" (*pratijñā-vibhāga*), that section on the Establishment of the Proposition itself serves as the basis for the sections on "Explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) and so forth;
since this cause also universally serves as a condition for those subsequent sections, it is likewise understood as general based on this meaning.
Regarding the marks: "to be free from all suffering" refers to all suffering of both the *pariccheda* (segmentary) and *pariṇāma* (evolutionary) types.
"Ultimate bliss" refers to the bliss of unsurpassed *bodhi* and great *nirvāṇa*. "Not seeking worldly things" means not hoping for the wealth and pleasures of humans and devas in future lives.
"Fame, profit, and honor" refers to not seeking the deceptive matters of the present life. This...

The seven [topics] below are its specific causes (*hetu*), because they serve as the causes for this treatise alone; and they serve as its specific conditions (*pratyaya*) with respect to the seven lower sections.

Regarding the second cause: within the three segments of the "Explanatory Section" (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*), it serves as the causal condition for two of those segments—namely, the "Revelation of the Correct Meaning" (*samyartha-pradarśana*) and the "Counteracting of Erroneous Attachments" (*viparyāsa-graha-vipakṣa*). Within the "Revelation of the Correct Meaning,"...
It is said: Based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates. These two gates each comprehensively encompass all dharmas.
One should know that this is precisely the fundamental meaning of all dharma-gates taught by the Tathāgata.

Because within these one mind and two gates there is not a single dharma or principle that is not subsumed, it is said that this is for the purpose of explaining the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata.

As for the second section, which counteracts erroneous attachments, it causes sentient beings to abandon the two types of deluded attachments to persons and dharmas; therefore, it is said to be for the sake of sentient beings.
This is because right understanding is free from error. As for the third cause, it serves as the causal condition for the third section within the "Explanatory Section" (vyākhyāna-bhāga).

That text analyzes the characteristics of setting out upon the path (*pratipatti-lakṣaṇa*) so that those of sharp faculties may decisively resolve their minds to advance toward the Great Vehicle and become capable of abiding in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Therefore, it says: "in order to cause [the planting of] roots of goodness."

...up to "because of not regressing from faith. The fourth cause is to serve as the causal condition for the four kinds of faith and the four practices at the beginning of the "Section on Cultivating Faith" below;
therefore, it says, "in order to cause the cultivation of faith. The fifth cause is for the sake of what is said at the end of the fourth practice below: "Furthermore, if..."

Although a person may cultivate faith, because they have many heavy karmic obstacles from previous lives, the text provides the causal conditions for five lines of practice that explain the method for removing these obstacles.
Therefore, it says this is "to demonstrate the skillful means for eliminating karmic obstacles and escaping the net of evil.
As for the sixth cause: it is so that one may understand how to practice *śamatha* (calm abiding).

From the passage beginning with "Contemplating as follows" up to "If cessation and contemplation are not complete, one will be unable to enter the path to Bodhi," there is a causal explanation spanning approximately three pages of text. Therefore, it says, "Cultivating cessation and contemplation... because of mental faults.
As for the seventh cause, it is because the end of the "Section on Cultivating Faith in Practice" states: "Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma..."
Below, the text concerning the eight practices for encouraging rebirth in the Pure Land serves as the causal context;
therefore, it says, "to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded recitation for being born before the Buddha," and so forth.

The eighth cause serves as the causal context for the fifth section, which concerns the benefits of encouraging practice; therefore, it says, "to demonstrate the benefits and encourage the cultivation of practice. Next—
The statement that there are such causes and conditions for composing this treatise constitutes the third section, which summarizes [the preceding].
The direct exposition of these causes and conditions has already been completed above.
Question: Since these teachings are fully contained within the Sūtras, why is it necessary to explain them again? Answer: Within the Sūtras...
Although this Dharma exists, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal, their receptions and understandings differ according to various conditions.

That is to say, when the Tathāgata is in the world, sentient beings possess sharp faculties, and the person who can preach possesses superior physical and mental karma; thus, when the perfect voice is uttered but once, those of diverse kinds understand it equally, and no treatise is required.
However, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there may be sentient beings who, by means of their own power, are able to hear extensively.
Regarding those who attain understanding: there are some sentient beings who, by their own power, attain much understanding from hearing little;
there are some sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding through extensive treatises;

and there are also sentient beings who find extensive textual discourse cumbersome and, delighting in concise retention (*saṃgraha*), are able to attain understanding through few words that encompass many meanings.
Thus, this treatise should be expounded in order to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.
Second, the removal of doubt consists of questions and answers. Regarding the question which states that "this Dharma is fully contained within the sūtras," it means:

Regarding the teachings explained based on the eight preceding causes—from the established meanings of the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" up to the benefits demonstrated in the "Section on Encouraging Practice"—all such dharmas are fully expounded in the Sūtras for the sake of enabling sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness.
Now, why is it that this treatise is further composed to restate those same dharmas? Is it not for...
Is it for the sake of seeking fame and profit? For this reason, he says, "Why is it necessary to explain it again?
This is a question raised from a state of doubt. The answer consists of three parts: a brief response, a detailed explanation, and a third part which is a brief concluding response.

Within the answer, the phrase "although this dharma exists within the Sūtras" refers back to the wording of the question. Regarding the roots and practices being unequal, there is a difference in how they are received and understood.

Regarding the "distinction based on conditions": this means removing their state of doubt. Although there is no separate dharma among what is taught in the sūtras and śāstras, those who receive and understand them differ in their faculties and practices.
Some rely on the sūtras and do not require the śāstras; others rely on the śāstras and do not require the sūtras.
Therefore, for the sake of such people, it was necessary to compose this treatise. Such is the meaning of the answer. Next, it will be extensively elucidated. At [the beginning of] the...

This section has two parts. First, it clarifies that when the Buddha was in the world, both the speaker and the listener were superior. Second, it reveals that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the faculties and conditions of beings became diverse.
Regarding the first part, the statement "when the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties" clarifies the superiority of the listeners.
The statement "the person who can speak possesses excellence in form, mind, and karma" reveals the superiority of the speaker. The phrase "the single utterance of the perfect voice" refers to...

The proponent is superior in establishing the doctrine; those of different classes who understand it equally are superior in being listeners. Thus, there is no need for further debate, as both have achieved the sense of victory.
These words constitute the "perfect sound" (*pariṣphuṭa-ghoṣa*), which is precisely the "single sound" (*eka-svara*). What is the meaning of this "single sound" being the "perfect sound"?

Since ancient times, the explanations of various masters have not been uniform. Some masters have said: "The Buddhas possess only the body of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kāya*), which forever transcends the myriad phenomena;
it is formless and soundless. It directly manifests immeasurable forms and sounds according to the capacities of beings, just as an empty valley has no sound yet emits an echo in response to a call.
Thus, speaking from the perspective of the Buddha himself, the absence of sound is one; however, regarding...
The *Jilun* (Treatise on the Pivot) states that the various sounds are not one and the same. What is the meaning of saying there is "one sound" or "perfect sound"?

It is because, within a single assembly at a single time, beings of different categories understand equally; according to their respective faculties and natures, each hears one sound and does not hear the other voices.
It is neither confused nor erroneous; it reveals the extraordinariness of this sound, and is therefore called "the single sound" (*ekasvara*).

This sound pervades the ten directions, and according to the faculties and ripening conditions of beings, there is nowhere it is not heard; thus it is called the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). This does not mean that it is like space, omnipresent and devoid of distinct melodic variations.
As the Sūtra says: "According to their respective kinds of sounds, he universally addresses all sentient beings. This is what is meant. Some say:
Regarding this, speaking from the perspective of the Buddha: he truly possesses form and sound. His voice is perfect and all-pervading;

it contains no distinction between the musical notes of *gong* and *shang*, nor any difference between the even (*ping*) and rising (*shang*) tones. Because there is no variation in melody, it is called "one sound" (*ekasvara*).

Because there is nothing it does not pervade, it is described as the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). It is simply because this perfect sound acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that [the teachings] accord with the differences in the faculties [of sentient beings].
It manifests as many distinct sounds, just as the full moon, though possessing only a single circular form, appears as many reflections according to the differences in the vessels that contain it;
one should know that the principle here is likewise. As a sutra says:
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind. Some say that the Tathāgata actually possesses many [voices].
Regarding sounds: all the speech and voices of all sentient beings are encompassed within the sound of the Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma.
Yet this Buddha-voice is unobstructed and unhindered; the one is all, and all is the one. All is the one.
Therefore, it is called "the single sound. One is all; therefore, it is called the "perfect sound. As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"The languages and dharmas of all sentient beings are fully expounded by a single word without exception; may they all understand this pure and subtle secret sound."

Because the Bodhisattva has, by virtue of this, first resolved their mind [on enlightenment], and because this Buddha-voice is inconceivable—it is not merely that one sound is all sounds, but it is also equally and universally pervasive regarding all phenomena.
For now, I shall briefly cite six pairs to manifest the characteristics of this equal and universal pervasiveness. The first is equality toward all sentient beings and all phenomena.
Second, they are equal to all lands in the ten directions and all kalpas of the three periods of time.
Third, they are equal to all Tathāgatas of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and all Buddhas of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Fourth, they are equal to the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the space-realm (*ākāśadhātu*). Fifth, they are equal to the realm of unimpeded mutual entry and the realm of immeasurable manifestation.
Sixth, it is equal to the realm of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dhātu*) and the realm of tranquil nirvāṇa.
This meaning is as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* within the context of the three kinds of non-obstruction.

Following each individual sound, these six pairs [of opposites] are present, yet their phonetic rhythms are never confused or disordered. If the sound were not to pervade these six pairs, then the sound would not be perfect. If...
If one were to lose the melodic contours through equal pervasiveness, then the "perfect" would not be "sound.

However, now, while maintaining the melodic contours through equal pervasiveness, and without moving from that pervasiveness, the various tones are produced. By this principle, the "perfect sound" (ghoṣa) is established.

This is not something that can be measured by the deliberations of the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), for it is the meaning of the sovereignty of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Such is the brief explanation of the meaning of the "single sound" (*ekasvara*).

Let us set aside further discussion and return to the explanation of the original text. Below this is the second section, which clarifies the differences in faculties and practices after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Within this, four distinct types of spiritual capacity (*indriya*) are presented. Of these, the first two attain understanding by relying on the sūtras, while the latter two attain understanding only by relying on the śāstras.
Regarding the first of these, it says: "Those who are able to attain understanding through extensive hearing by means of their own power."
This refers to one who, by relying on extensive scriptural study, attains understanding of the Buddha’s intent without requiring formal treatises; hence, it is called "self-power.

Regarding the second point, the phrase "also by self-power, hearing little yet understanding much" means that one need not necessarily have heard the words and phrases of many scriptures extensively, yet is able to deeply understand the underlying meaning and intent of those scriptures; as this too does not require treatises, it is called "self-power."

Regarding the third point, the statement that one lacks the power of one's own mind means that one cannot understand [the teachings] by relying solely on the Buddha’s sūtras; therefore, it is said that one lacks such power.
It is only by means of treatises such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* that one can finally comprehend the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) taught in the Buddha’s sūtras;

hence, it is said that understanding is attained through reliance on the extensive treatises (*śāstra*). Regarding the fourth point, the statement "furthermore, because the texts of the extensive treatises are numerous" refers to...

As for those who are "distracted": although they possess sharp faculties, they cannot endure prolixity. Such persons rely solely on treatises that are concise in wording yet rich in meaning, thereby gaining a profound understanding of the intent of what is taught in the Buddha’s sūtras.
Therefore, it is said that their minds delight in *dhāraṇī*—that which condenses vast meanings into few words and enables one to grasp the understanding.
Among these four types, the first three are not the subjects of this work; the subject of this work is as follows:
Regarding the fourth person: as follows below, this is the third summary conclusion. The term "thus" (*evam*) refers collectively to the four types of persons mentioned previously;
from here on, the treatise specifically addresses the fourth person to conclude and clarify the necessity for composing this treatise.
This present treatise consists of only one fascicle, yet it universally encompasses the essential meaning of all the sūtras. Therefore...
This is because it is said to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.
That fourth category, the class of those who delight in *dhāraṇī*, must rely upon this treatise to attain realization of the Path; for this reason, it is said that this treatise should be expounded.
The section on causes and conditions has already been explained. Next, the section establishing the doctrine will be explained. The Mahāyāna, in general, is said to be of two kinds.
What are these two? First is the phenomenon (*dharma*); second is the meaning (*artha*). That which is called "phenomenon" refers to the mind of sentient beings.
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed.
Why is this? Because the aspect of the suchness of this mind reveals the essence of the Mahāyāna;

and the aspect of the arising and ceasing through causes and conditions of this mind can reveal the essence, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna itself. As for what is called "meaning," there are three kinds.
What are the three? First is the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*), which refers to the fact that the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Second is the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*), which refers to the fact that the tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent qualities (*guṇa*). Third is the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahat*).
Because it is able to produce all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects; because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted;
and because all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.

The second section explains the division on establishing the thesis (*siddhānta-vibhāga*). This passage contains two parts: first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one (from "Mahā" onwards);
second, the formal exposition, which establishes two topical headings (*dvāra*), namely *dharma* and *artha*. *Dharma* refers to the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of the Mahāyāna;
*artha* refers to the names and meanings of the Mahāyāna. First, regarding the establishment of *dharma*, it initiates the beginning of the subsequent explanation.

Regarding the passage on the essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): next, as for the establishment of the meaning, the section beginning with "Furthermore, regarding the self-substance and characteristics of True Suchness" (*tathatā*) and following is the text that explains this meaning.
Within the initial establishment of the doctrine, there are also two types of establishment:

first, the general establishment based on the substance itself, which gives rise to the initial general explanation in the subsequent commentary; second, the specific establishment according to the gates, which gives rise to the subsequent statement "True Suchness... and so forth.

The section beginning with "That which is such" (tathatā) provides a detailed explanation of the text. Regarding the initial statement, "What is called 'dharmas' refers to the mind of sentient beings":
the intrinsic nature is termed "dharma. Now, within the Mahāyāna, all dharmas lack distinct intrinsic natures;
they take only the single mind as their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said that what are called "dharmas" refer to the mind of sentient beings. This mind, moreover, subsumes [all things].
"Everything" (sarva) indicates that the Mahāyāna Dharma differs from the Hīnayāna Dharma. This is because this mind universally encompasses all phenomena (*dharma*);
the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is solely the one mind. This is unlike the Hīnayāna, where all phenomena are said to each have their own distinct intrinsic nature;
therefore, the one mind is taught as the Mahāyāna Dharma. As for the phrase "For what reason? and so forth, it establishes [the categories] separately according to their gates. This...
A single passage contains two meanings: with respect to what precedes, it explains the general meaning; with respect to what follows, it establishes the specific categories.

Nevertheless, the mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are one. Since the meaning of the Mahāyāna is vast, for what reason does [the text] directly rely upon this mind to reveal the meaning of the Mahāyāna?
Therefore, it is asked: "For what reason? The subsequent explanation clarifies the intent: although the mental dharmas are one, they possess two gates.
Within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) lies the essence of the Mahāyāna; within the gate of Arising and Ceasing lie the essence, characteristics, and function.

Since the meaning of the Mahāyāna does not exceed these three, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed by relying on the One Mind. As for the phrase "the True Suchness of this mind," it is a general [statement].
The mention of the "Gate of Suchness" (tathatā-mukha) introduces the following passage: "That which is one dharma-realm...

Next, the mention of "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the characteristics of suchness, introducing the following passage: "Furthermore, suchness, based on verbal expression and conceptual discrimination, is of two kinds...

The statement "this is the mind of arising and ceasing" (citta-utpāda-nirodha) provides a general overview of the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing," introducing the following passage: "Based on suchness..."

"Because of the *ālayavijñāna*, there is the mind of arising and ceasing"—this refers to the subsequent passage. To speak of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) means they are the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing;

this introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "Furthermore, the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing. Next, to speak of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) means they are the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
this introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "Furthermore, as for arising and ceasing. To speak of "that which can demonstrate the Mahāyāna" [is the purpose].
"Self-substance" (svabhāva) refers to the intrinsically enlightened mind (prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna) within the gate of arising and ceasing;
it is the substance of arising and ceasing and the cause of arising and ceasing, and for this reason it resides within the gate of arising and ceasing.

Nevertheless, there is a profound reason why the "substance of the Mahāyāna" is spoken of directly in the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), whereas it is termed "self-substance" in the gate of arising and ceasing. This will be explained further below.
The meaning is self-evident. Regarding the terms "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "function" (*vṛtti*), they contain two senses.

First, they indicate the characteristics of the immeasurable virtuous qualities inherent within the *tathāgatagarbha*; this is the meaning of "greatness of characteristics. Furthermore, they indicate the inconceivable karmic functions of the *tathāgatagarbha*;
this is the meaning of "greatness of function. Second, they refer to the defiled characteristics produced by *tathatā*, which are termed "characteristics."
The pure functioning arising from *tathatā* (suchness) is called "function. As the text below states: "In the pure dharmas of *tathatā*, there is in reality no defilement;
yet because they are perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the appearance of defilement arises. In the defiled dharmas of ignorance, there is fundamentally no pure activity;
yet because they are perfumed by *tathatā*, the function of purity arises. This concludes the section on establishing the categories of dharmas.

It is already present before us. Below this is the second section, the Chapter on Establishing the Propositions (*sthāpana-varga*). This also contains two parts: first, the elucidation of the Great Meaning (*mahārtha*);

second, the manifestation of the Meaning of the Vehicle (*yānārtha*). These also serve to introduce the text of the subsequent explanation; when one reaches those passages, they will correspond to one another.

Within the Great Meaning, the "Greatness of Essence" (*tattva-mahat*) resides in the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), while the two "Greatnesses of Characteristic and Function" (*lakṣaṇa-vṛtti-mahat*) reside in the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
The Gate of Arising and Ceasing also possesses its own essence; however, because the essence follows from the characteristics, it is not explained separately.
To say that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fully endowed with immeasurable essential merits (*dharmas*) refers, within the two types of *garbhas*, to the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Among the two types of *garbhas*, this is the *tathāgatagarbha* that is capable of encompassing the meaning of essential merits and the meaning of the greatness of function.
This shall be analyzed in detail later in the commentary. Regarding the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*), there are two phrases.
"Because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden upon" explains the meaning of vehicle by establishing the fruit in relation to the cause.
"Because all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata" explains the meaning of vehicle by taking the cause as the basis in relation to the fruit.
△ In the third section, the "Explanatory Division" (vyākhyāna-bhāga), there are two parts according to the text: first, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent;
second, the actual explanation. Within the actual explanation, there are three parts: first, stating the number to provide a general heading; second, opening the chapters according to that number;
third, providing a detailed interpretation according to those chapters.
The section on establishing the thesis has been explained. Next, the section on interpretation will be explained. There are three types within the section on interpretation.

What are these three? First, the revelation of the correct meaning; second, the counteraction of erroneous attachments; and third, the differentiation of the characteristics of those who have set out upon the path.
Within the opening chapter, the phrase "to reveal the correct principle" refers to the actual explanation of that which was established in the section on the "Establishment of the Meaning.
The phrase "the characteristics of counteracting false attachments and setting out upon the path" clarifies the gateway of departing from the erroneous and proceeding toward the correct.
