Because, based upon the defiled mind, one is able to perceive and manifest, falsely grasping at objects and thereby contravening the nature of equality. Because all phenomena...
It is eternally quiescent and devoid of any sign of arising. Because ignorance lacks awakening, it falsely opposes the Dharma;
thus, it is unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all worldly objects.
The sixth section clarifies the meaning of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). In the exoteric gate (*vyañjana-mukha*), they are termed the "two obstacles" (*dvividha-āvaraṇa*);

within the esoteric gate (*saṃdhi-mukha*), they are termed the "two hindrances" (*dvividha-vibandha*). This meaning is fully explained as it appears in the chapter on the two obstacles; here, in this text, the esoteric gate is discussed.

Within this, there are two parts. The first part divides the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). Below this, the reason for this is explained. Regarding the meaning of "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-citta*) mentioned at the beginning:

this reveals the six types of defiled minds. As for "fundamental wisdom" (*mūla-jñāna*), because it is a wisdom that illuminates quiescence yet contradicts [the state of] quiescence itself, it is called the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the meaning of "ignorance" (*avidyā*): it refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) in the world.
The "knowledge of karma" is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Because ignorance is deluded and non-discriminative, it contradicts the discriminative knowledge of the world;
based on this principle, it is termed an "obstruction to knowledge. In the explanation of the reason [for this], this meaning is precisely revealed.

Regarding the statement that "by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest, falsely grasping at objects," this briefly cites the manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
"Consciousness-cognition cognizes" refers to that which contradicts the nature of equality; it contradicts the fundamental wisdom in which subject and object are equal.

This is the explanation of the meaning of the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "Because all phenomena are eternally quiescent and lack the characteristic of arising" raises the dharmatā (the true nature of phenomena) as that which is deluded by ignorance.
"Because ignorance is non-awakened and falsely opposes the dharma" reveals the delusion of ignorance.

Regarding the meaning of *dharmatā*: "Therefore, one cannot attain [it], up to and including the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*)—this clearly explains how it contradicts the meaning of worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*).

(Separate Record) Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), there are briefly two categories: first, those common to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), namely the ten afflictions (*kleśa*).
That which causes one to wander in saṃsāra and obstructs the fruit of nirvāṇa is called the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The specific hindrance of bodhisattvas consists of delusions such as the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which are confused regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and obstruct the fruit of bodhi; this is called the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This section is as explained in other sūtras and śāstras. Second, all minds that move with conceptualization and grasp at signs contradict the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-yoniśo-jñāna*).

The nature of quiescence is called the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Fundamental ignorance, being deluded and lacking awakening, contravenes the function of the wisdom of suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*) that discerns reality;
this is called the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). In this treatise, the meaning is explained according to the latter category.

Therefore, it is said that the six types of defiled minds are called "obstructions of affliction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the stage of abiding in ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is termed the "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
However, this is based on their correspondence: ignorance should obstruct intuitive wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), whereas defiled minds obstruct conventional cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).
Why is it not otherwise? Because it is not necessarily so. The sense of "not necessarily so" is as explained by the treatise itself.
The second section, the extensive explanation of the meaning of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, is now complete.
△ Third, the extensive explanation of the characteristics of arising and ceasing from the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" above. This contains two parts:
first, clarifying the coarse and subtle characteristics of arising and ceasing; second, revealing the meaning of coarse and subtle arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of characteristics regarding the analysis of arising and ceasing. What are these two? First is the coarse, because it is associated with the mind;
second is the subtle, because it is dissociated from the mind. Moreover, the coarsest among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
the subtle among the coarse and the coarse among the subtle are the realms of Bodhisattvas; and the subtlest among the subtle is that of the Buddhas.
Regarding the objective spheres (*viṣaya*):
the first and second [sections] each have two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the coarse and the subtle; second, the classification according to persons.

Within the first of these, there are also two: a general heading and a detailed explanation. In the detailed explanation, the statement "first, because the coarse is associated with the mind" refers to the six [consciousnesses].

Among the various defilements (*kleśa*), the first three are associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*); their characteristics are coarse and manifest, and thus they are described in the sūtras as "the arising and ceasing of signs.
As for the second category, those that are subtle and dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*), these refer to the latter three defilements of the mind.

This is not [a case of] dissociation (*viprayukta*). It lacks the coarse and manifest characteristics of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); its substance is subtle and flows constantly without interruption.
In the Sūtras, it is called "successive arising and ceasing" (*prabandha-utpāda-nirodha*). As the Ten-Scroll Sūtra says: "Consciousness has two kinds of cessation. What are the two?
First, the cessation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*); second, the cessation of continuity (*prabandha-nirodha*). Arising and abiding are likewise. (4)
The *Sūtra* states: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravāha*) and arising as manifestation (*nimitta*).
Cessation is likewise. In the *Sūtra*, these two types are mentioned by name alone, without specifically clarifying their characteristics.

Therefore, the Master of the Treatise now distinguishes between these two types—coarse and subtle—by means of the principles of association (*saṃprayoga*) and non-association (*asaṃprayoga*). [This is] in response to [the question of] persons.
Among the categories of discrimination, that which is coarse within the coarse refers to the first two of the three previously mentioned.
That which is subtle within the coarse refers to the last one of these three. This is because the first two among the former both reside within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse; therefore, it is known by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Among the former, middle, and latter [stages], the first is the seventh consciousness;

its mode of activity is not coarse, and thus it is not understood by ordinary beings. Of the latter, middle, and first [stages], the first two can manifest and can see, involving a distinction between subject and object;
therefore, they are known by Bodhisattvas. The final one involves no differentiation between subject and object; therefore, only a Buddha can understand it.
Furthermore, these two kinds of arising and ceasing exist based upon the perfuming of ignorance; that is to say, they depend upon causes and conditions.

"Depending upon causes" refers to the meaning of non-awakening. "Depending upon conditions" refers to the meaning of falsely constructing objective realms. If the cause ceases, then the condition [ceases].
Cessation. Because the cause ceases, the non-associated mind ceases; because the condition ceases, the associated mind ceases. Question: If the mind ceases, how can there be continuity?
If there is continuity, how can one speak of ultimate cessation? Answer:

What is called "cessation" refers only to the cessation of the mental characteristics (*citta-lakṣaṇa*), not the cessation of the essence of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*). It is like wind which possesses the characteristic of movement depending upon water; if the water...
When it ceases, the characteristic of wind is severed and has no basis for support. Because water does not cease, the characteristic of wind continues;

it is only because the wind ceases that the characteristic of motion also ceases accordingly, yet it is not that the water itself ceases. Ignorance is likewise: it moves in dependence upon the substance of the mind.
If the substance of the mind were to perish, then sentient beings would be severed and have no basis for support. Because its substance does not perish, the mind can continue in succession;
it is only because delusion perishes that the characteristics of the mind perish accordingly, but it is not the cognitive wisdom of the mind that perishes.

The second section clarifies the meaning of arising and ceasing. This contains two parts: first, it clarifies the conditions for arising; second, it reveals the meaning of cessation. Within the first part, there are also two sections:
first, it clarifies the universal conditions; second, it reveals the specific causes. Generally speaking, these refer to the two consciousnesses—the coarse and the subtle.
All arise based on the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*). Therefore, it is said that there are two kinds of arising and ceasing.
These exist based upon the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of ignorance. To distinguish them specifically: based on the cause of ignorance, the non-associated mind (*viprayukta-citta*) arises;

based on the condition of objective realms (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), the associated mind (*saṃprayukta-citta*) arises. Thus, it is said that "depending on the cause" refers to the meaning of non-awakening (*abodha*), while "depending on the condition" [refers to the objective realm].

This is because it has the sense of falsely constructing objects (the *Bieji* states: "The sense of non-awakening refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*); 'falsely constructing objects' refers to the objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness).

To explain according to their full meaning, each has two causes. As the four-fascicle sutra says: "O Mahamati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).
Taking up various sensory objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination (*parikalpita*) are [the causes of the object-perceiving consciousness]."
Regarding the phrase "the cause of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena," the commentary explains:
"Inconceivable perfuming" refers to ignorance being able to perfume the *tathatā* (Suchness). Because it is able to perfume that which cannot be perfumed, it is called "inconceivable perfuming.
"Inconceivable transformation" refers to *tathatā* undergoing perfuming by ignorance; because it undergoes transformation despite being incapable of change, it is so named. Thus...

It is called the "inconceivable transformation. This perfuming and this transformation are extremely subtle and hidden; therefore, the aspect of the manifest consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*) that arises from them is also subtle.

Within it, there are also the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). However, because the coarse is cited as inclusive of the subtle, it is simply termed the "manifest consciousness.
Regarding the "grasping of various objects" (*viṣaya*), these are the various objective realms grasped by the manifest consciousness, which are capable of stirring the mind.

Because the seven consciousness-waves arise from the ocean [of the ālayavijñāna]. Regarding "the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination": this very manifesting-consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna) is termed "false discrimination.
Since time immemorial, it has never been separated from conceptualization; therefore, it is called "beginningless false discrimination," as stated in the passage above.
Because it has never been separated from conceptualization since the very beginning, it is called "beginningless ignorance" (*anādikāla-avidyā*).
One should know that the false imagination (*vikalpa*) herein is likewise so. As the ten-fascicle *Sūtra* states: "The Ālayavijñāna is known as the characteristic of cognition;
its essential nature and characteristics are like a hair-net appearing in empty space, the objective sphere of impure wisdom. By means of this path..."

From the perspective of principle, these are false imaginings. Those various objects and this false imagining permeate the ocean of the mind’s own-characteristic, causing the waves of the seven consciousnesses to arise.

Because false imaginings and objects are coarse and manifest, the discerning consciousness of affairs (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) that they give rise to has coarse and manifest modes of activity, forming the associated mind.
This is intended to clarify that the cause of the manifest consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) is inconceivable.
It arises due to the perfuming of deliberation (*manas*) and abides by virtue of inconceivable transformation.

The consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) arises by taking various sense objects as conditions and abides by virtue of the perfuming of false conceptualization (*parikalpa*). In this treatise, however, we take only the conditions for arising;

therefore, among the subtle [consciousnesses], only the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā*) is mentioned, while among the coarse [consciousnesses], only the condition of objective spheres (*viṣaya*) is cited.

(Additional Note) Furthermore, the four-fascicle *Sūtra* states: "Mahāmati, if those various unreal and false [constructions] that veil the true consciousness are extinguished, then all sense-faculties and consciousnesses are extinguished;
this is called the extinction of marks (*nimitta-nirodha*). As for the extinction of continuity (*saṃtati-nirodha*):
when the causes of continuity are extinguished, continuity is extinguished; when that from which it proceeds and its objects of perception are extinguished, continuity is extinguished."
Why is this so? Because it is that upon which [the other] depends. "Dependence" refers to the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
"Conditioning" refers to the false conceptualization of the objects of consciousness, such as the manifestations of one's own mind.

This sutra makes this statement from the perspective of the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the treatise (*śāstra*) speaks according to specific meanings as previously explained. If one were to discuss the causes and conditions for arising in a general sense...
Consciousnesses each have four kinds of causes and conditions. As stated in the Ten-Scroll Sūtra: "There are four causes and conditions for the arising of visual consciousness.
What are the four? First, because one does not realize one's own internal body and thus grasps at external objects;
second, because from time immemorial there has been the habitual attachment to false discrimination regarding the objects of form and the proliferation of conceptual play."
Third, because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is such. Fourth, because of the desire to see various forms and appearances.
The four-fascicle sutra states: "Eye-consciousness arises due to four causes and conditions: namely, the non-awakening to the grasping of what is manifested by one's own mind;
the attachment to the habitual tendencies of form resulting from beginningless false delusions; the intrinsic nature of consciousness itself; and the desire to see various [forms]."

These various colors and forms are called the four kinds of causal conditions for the place where the water flows. From the *ālayavijñāna*, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise.
Regarding the statement "non-awakening to the grasping of what is manifested by one’s own mind": this clarifies that fundamental ignorance (*mūlavidyā*) is the cause.

As for their coarse characteristics, they are manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsavijñāna*); they do not exist outside of consciousness, because they are subsumed within one’s own mind. This is called non-awakening.
This means that ignorance does not perceive that the objects of form are not external; therefore, it is able to give rise to the visual consciousness, causing it to grasp them as external.
This constitutes the first cause. As for the statement "beginningless falsehood... up to attachment," this reveals the cause of beginningless perfuming by delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

That is to say, the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) has fundamentally grasped and attached to the objects of form; it is due to these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) [that such perceptions arise].

It is capable of producing eye-consciousness so that it may apprehend the object-field of form (*rūpa*). When we speak of the "nature of consciousness," this reveals its cause within its own category (*svajāti-hetu*):
due to the self-nature discrimination of a preceding eye-consciousness, subsequent eye-consciousness arises through that perfuming (*vāsanā*) with a self-nature identical to the former.
When we speak of "desiring to see various forms and characteristics," this reveals the cause of the perfuming of names and speech (*nāma-vyavahāra-vāsanā-hetu*).

This means that while the preceding visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is able to perceive the characteristics of forms, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes this [visual consciousness] as its object and is thus able to perceive the visual consciousness.

Through the conceptualization of mental discourse (*manojalpa*), it grasps and clings to the desire to see. As it has been explained regarding visual consciousness, the other consciousnesses may be understood by analogy.
If the cause ceases, next the meaning of cessation is revealed. This section contains two parts: first, a direct explanation; second, a series of questions and answers to resolve doubts.

Regarding the statement, "If the cause ceases, then the conditions cease," this means that whenever one attains the antidote at any stage, the object of ignorance—the cause—ceases, and the conditions accordingly cease. Because the cause has ceased, they are no longer associated.
Regarding the cessation of the mind: the three types of dissociated minds arise based on ignorance as their immediate cause;
therefore, when ignorance ceases, they also cease accordingly. Regarding the cessation of the associated mind due to the cessation of conditions:

the three types of defiled associated minds arise based on objects as their immediate condition; therefore, when objects cease, they also cease accordingly. This is the beginning and end [of the process].
The principle of arising and ceasing clarifies the meaning of two kinds of birth and death; it does not refer to the meaning of momentary (kṣaṇika) arising and ceasing.

Below this is the second section, consisting of a dialogue to dispel doubts, first with a question and then with an answer. In the question, the phrase "If the mind ceases, how can there be continuity?
is asked in response to the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), as stated in the ten-fascicle version of the Sūtra.
If the ālayavijñāna were to cease, it would not differ from the conceptual proliferation of the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists. The various non-Buddhists say:

"When consciousness that continues [through rebirth] ceases—having departed from all objective spheres—and once that continuing consciousness has ceased, then all consciousnesses are extinguished. Mahāmati, [this is their claim].
If the continuous consciousness were to cease, then all consciousnesses from beginningless time would have to cease. This [passage] precisely clarifies the doctrine of certain non-Buddhists:

just as when one is born into the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) or enters the Attainment of Cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one is separated from all objective spheres and the continuous consciousness ceases;
because the root has ceased, the branches also follow in cessation. The Tathāgata refutes this, saying: "If those sentient beings..."

Regarding the claim that when one enters the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)—the continuity of sentient beings—is extinguished, such that the seeds of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and so forth are extinguished accordingly and no further consciousnesses should arise from it;
yet, upon emerging from that state, various consciousnesses do indeed arise again.

One should know that when entering the state of non-conception, the continuity-consciousness (*saṃtativijñāna*) is not extinguished. This is how [the opponent's position] is refuted. Now, within this treatise:

Based on this, one asks: if the substance of the mind were to cease when entering the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), how could it resume?

Therefore, it is said: "If the mind were to cease, how could it continue? Conversely, if the substance of the mind does not cease when entering those states but continues to exist, by what means could this continuity be permanently extinguished? Therefore, it is asked: "How can you explain this?"
"Ultimately extinguished. The answer consists of three parts: the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis. First, regarding the principle:

when it is said that "consciousnesses are extinguished" upon entering states such as the non-conceptual (*asaṃjñika*), this refers only to the extinction of the characteristics of gross consciousnesses;

it does not mean the extinction of the essence of the *ālayavijñāna*. Therefore, it is said that "only the mental characteristics are extinguished. Furthermore, as stated above, because the cause is extinguished, [the effect does not arise].

Regarding the cessation of the associated mind (*saṃprayukta-citta*): this refers only to the cessation of the mental factors such as karma within the mind, and does not mean that the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the mind-essence itself ceases.
This distinction between the two types of cessation is specifically clarified in the analogy: "Just as wind exists dependent upon water and possesses the characteristic of movement."
This is a metaphor for the wind of ignorance moving in dependence upon the mind. If the water were extinguished, the wind would be cut off and have no basis to rely upon.

That the characteristics of the wind continue in succession because the water is not extinguished is a metaphor for when one enters such states as the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

The essence of the mind is indestructible; therefore, the various consciousnesses continue in succession. This answers the first question. As for the statement that "only because the wind ceases does the moving aspect cease accordingly":
when one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, ignorance is eternally extinguished; consequently, the movement of the marks of karma and so forth also ceases and is exhausted accordingly.
Yet, its own-characteristic—the essence of the mind—is not extinguished; thus it is said that it is not like the extinction of water. This is...
The answer to the subsequent question clarifies ultimate cessation. Within the synthesis, the sequence synthesizes the two preceding meanings.

Regarding "the cessation of mental wisdom": the nature of spiritual understanding is termed "mental wisdom. As the previous passage states, "the nature of wisdom is indestructible," this clarifies the meaning that its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not perish.
The remaining passages may be understood accordingly. Question: Is this consciousness’s own characteristic invariably...?

It arises from defiled conditions. Should it also possess the quality of not arising from conditions? If it were exclusively produced by defiled conditions, then when those defiled dharmas are exhausted, it would naturally cease along with them.
On the other hand, if it does not cease because its own characteristic does not arise from defiled conditions, then it would exist spontaneously.
Furthermore, if its own characteristic were also to cease, it would be identical to the view of nihilism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi). This being so—
If one claims that its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not extinguished, it would be equivalent to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). To this, some reply:

"The essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is a dharma of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*). It arises solely as differentiated by karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, when karma and afflictions are exhausted, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is entirely extinguished.
Nevertheless, in the state of Buddhahood, there is also the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which corresponds to the two practices of merit and wisdom (*puṇya* and *prajñā*)."
Regarding pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) is identical in both cases. It is for this reason that it is said that the mind reaches the fruit of Buddhahood.
Some say that the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the essence of mind, in its entirety, is produced by that ignorance (*avidyā*).
This refers to the arising of movement and stillness, not to the transformation of non-existence into existence. Therefore, the movement of this mind arises because of ignorance.
This is called the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*). This moving mind is, from the very beginning, the mind itself; it is also its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of this characteristic does not arise from ignorance (*avidyā*). Nevertheless, this mind moved by ignorance also possesses the principle of mutual production within its own kind.
Therefore, there is no fault of being spontaneous (*svabhāva*), and there is the principle of non-extinction. When ignorance is exhausted—
The moving aspect perishes accordingly, and the mind follows initial awakening back to its original source.

Some say that both masters’ explanations possess reason, as they both rely on what is taught in the sacred scriptures. The first master’s explanation accords with the intent of the *Yogācāra* (the *Separate Record* states:
"it relies on the explicit teaching"), while the latter master’s meaning accords with the intent of the *Awakening of Faith* (the *Separate Record* states: "it relies on the hidden teaching"). And...

Furthermore, one must not grasp the meaning according to the literal expression. Why is this so? If one grasps the meaning as stated in the former [passage], that constitutes the clinging to a self of phenomena (*dharmātman*).
If one grasps the meaning as stated in the latter [passage], that is called the view of a self of persons (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*).

Moreover, if one clings to the former meaning, one falls into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); if one clings to the latter meaning, one falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). One should know these two.
The meanings are all ineffable; yet, though ineffable, they can also be explained, because although they are not thus, they are not otherwise.
Within the detailed exposition of the two divisions inside the Section on Arising and Ceasing, the first, which is the formal detailed exposition itself, has already been concluded above.
△ From here below is the second section, which clarifies through further explanation by means of causal statements. Why is this? As stated in the preceding text: "This consciousness has two meanings:

it is able to encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena. While the meaning of its capacity to encompass has already been explained at length, the meaning of its capacity to give rise [to phenomena] has not yet been made clear.
Therefore, from here below, this meaning is extensively revealed. There are five parts within the text.
First, the enumeration of the number as a general heading; second, the listing of names according to that number; third, a general explanation of the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*);
fourth, a specific elucidation of the characteristics of perfuming; and fifth, an explanation of the meaning of exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that function through the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*), defiled and pure dharmas arise without interruption.
What are these four? First is the pure dharma, which is called *tathatā* (suchness). Second is the cause of all defilements, which is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Third is the deluded mind, which is termed the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*). Fourth are the deluded objects, namely the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
The enumeration and listing of these names are clear from the textual context.
Regarding the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*): it is like a worldly garment that, though actually devoid of fragrance, comes to possess a scent because it has been perfumed by someone with incense.

This is likewise the case here: the pure phenomenon of *tathatā* (suchness), though actually devoid of defilement, manifests the appearance of defilement simply because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Conversely, the defiled phenomenon of ignorance, though its actual nature is pure, [manifests] simply because of *tathatā*.
Because it is thus perfumed, there is the function of purity.

Within the third [section], first the metaphor, then the application. In the application, the phrase "the pure dharma of true suchness" refers to the meaning of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
The phrase "the defiled dharma of ignorance" refers to the meaning of non-enlightenment (*an-awakening*). This is truly because a single consciousness contains these two meanings. Furthermore...

They mutually perfume one another, universally giving rise to both the defiled and the pure. This meaning correctly explains the significance of "inconceivable perfuming" and "inconceivable transformation" as taught in the original sūtra.
Question: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that it must possess four conditions to be capable of receiving perfuming.
Therefore, it is said that permanent dharmas cannot receive perfuming (*vāsanā*). Why, then, is it stated here that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is perfumed?
The explanation is as follows: there are two types of perfuming. That treatise speaks of perfuming in terms of what is conceivable;
thus, it says that permanent dharmas do not receive perfuming. This treatise clarifies inconceivable perfuming; therefore, it says that ignorance perfumes True Suchness.
The manner in which true suchness (*tathatā*) perfumes ignorance (*avidyā*) and the manner in which it manifests the mind (*manas*) are different; therefore, they are not contradictory.

However, within this text, that which is called "true suchness" refers to the intrinsically pure original enlightenment (*prakṛti-viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*) within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*); thus, it possesses the sense of "perfuming.
This does not refer to the true suchness within the gate of true suchness (*tathatā-dvāra*), because within the gate of true suchness, the sense of being "that which gives rise to" is not taught.
△ Hereafter follows the fourth section, the specific exposition. This contains two parts: first, defilement; second, purity.
How does the perfuming that gives rise to defiled phenomena continue without interruption? It is said:

because there is ignorance based upon the *tathatā* (suchness), and because there exists the cause of defiled phenomena—namely, ignorance—it perfumes the *tathatā*. Because of this perfuming, [defiled phenomena] arise.

The deluded mind: because there is a deluded mind, it perfumes ignorance; because one does not understand the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena, unawakened thoughts arise, manifesting delusive objects.

Because these delusive objects serve as conditions for defiled dharmas, they in turn perfume the deluded mind, causing it to become attached through thought and thereby creating various karmas and undergoing all manner of suffering of body and mind. This perfuming by delusive objects...
The meaning of "habitual cultivation" (*vāsanā*) is twofold. What are the two? First, the habitual cultivation that increases mindfulness;
second, the habitual cultivation that increases grasping (*upādāna*). The meaning of the habitual cultivation of the deluded mind is also twofold. What are the two?
First, the fundamental habitual cultivation of the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*), which causes Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of birth and death.

Second, it is the perfuming that increases the *vicitra-vijñapti-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of various perceived objects), because it enables one to undergo the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings.
There are two meanings to the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā*). What are these two? First is the fundamental perfuming, because it can bring about the realization of the *karma-vijñāna*.
Second is the perfuming of views and craving (*dṛṣṭi-tṛṣṇā*) that arises from it, because it can bring about the realization of the *vicitra-vijñapti-vastu-vijñāna*.

Because of this meaning, there are also two [aspects] within defilement: first the question, and then the answer. Within the answer, there are two parts: a brief clarification and an extensive exposition.

In the brief clarification, the statement that "ignorance exists based on the *tathatā*-dharma" reveals the essence of both the perfuming agent (*paribhāvaka*) and the perfumed object (*paribhāvya*). This is because...
"Unenlightened ignorance perfumes True Suchness" refers to the meaning of fundamental unenlightened ignorance perfuming [the mind].
"Because of this perfuming, there is deluded mind" means that based on the perfuming of unenlightened ignorance, there arises the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*).

Because this deluded mind in turn perfumes unenlightened ignorance, it increases its lack of understanding; thus, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśavijñāna*) are formed. Therefore, it is said: "non-awakening thoughts."

The arising of present false objects (the *Bi ji* states: "unawakened thought arises—this is the aspect of transformation; the manifestation of false objects—this is the aspect of manifestation") means that these objects, in turn, perfume the manifest consciousness (*xiàn shí*).
Therefore, it is said that they perfume the deluded mind. "Causing it to become attached through thought" refers to the arising of the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).
"Creating various kinds of karma" refers to the arising of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). "Experiencing all suffering" refers to receiving [retribution] based on that karma.
This is the result. In the subsequent detailed exposition, the three preceding meanings are explained extensively, proceeding from the end. First, the objective realm (*viṣaya*) is clarified.
"Increasing mindfulness" means that by the power of the objective realm, the conceptual mindfulness of dharma-attachment within the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) is increased.

"Increasing grasping" means that the afflictive hindrances of the four types of grasping (*catvāra upādānāni*) are increased. Within the perfuming of the deluded mind, there is the root of the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness).

Regarding "original perfuming": this karmic consciousness can perfume ignorance, causing delusion regarding the signless and giving rise to the continuous succession of the evolving aspect (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) and the manifesting aspect (*nirbhāsa-lakṣaṇa*).

When those of the Three Vehicles emerge from the triple world, although they have abandoned the coarse suffering of the segmented consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), they still undergo the *ālayavijñāna*’s suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) within the transformational body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Therefore, it is said that they undergo the suffering of arising and ceasing associated with the Three Vehicles.

Discussing this comprehensively: although [the seeds] have existed since beginningless time, it is for the sake of distinguishing between the two types of perfuming—the coarse and the subtle—that they are described in relation to the stage when one has already departed from coarse suffering.

Regarding the perfuming of the *vikaḷpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), this is explained in reference to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and concerns the suffering of fragmentation (*pariccheda-duḥkha*).
Within the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā*), the "fundamental perfuming" refers to the fundamental [ignorance].

This is awakening. Regarding the "perfuming of the views and attachments arising [from it]": the views and attachments of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising from ignorance are precisely the meaning of the "unawakened" state at the branch-level.

(Separate Record) As for the statement regarding the "perfuming of the discriminative consciousness of phenomena that increases": this refers to the views, attachments, and afflictions of the mental consciousness.
Because it is increased by affliction (*kleśa*), one is able to undergo the fruits of karma bound to the three realms; therefore, it is said that "ordinary beings are bound by the suffering of karma.

Regarding the statement within the section on the permeation of ignorance (*avidyā*) concerning "fundamental permeation," this refers to fundamental ignorance permeating True Suchness (*tathatā*), causing it to stir its thoughts;
this is called the "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*). Therefore, it is said that "it accomplishes karma."
This refers to the meaning of *vijñāna* (consciousness). Regarding the phrase "the perfuming of views and craving that arise":

it means that the views and cravings arising from fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) perfume the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), giving rise to coarse discrimination; therefore, it is said that this establishes the meaning of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of discriminated objects).
How is it that the perfuming gives rise to the uninterrupted arising of pure dharmas? It is because the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) exists;

it is able to perfume ignorance. By the power of the causes and conditions of this perfuming, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*.
Because this deluded mind possesses these causes and conditions of weariness and seeking, it immediately perfumes *tathatā*, whereby one gains self-confidence in one’s own nature.
Knowing that the mind is falsely moving and that no external objects exist, one cultivates the dharma of detachment.
Because one knows with suchness that no external objects exist, one employs various skillful means to initiate corresponding practices—neither grasping nor recollecting them.
Eventually, through the power of long-term cultivation, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise; because it does not arise, there are no objects.

They cease accordingly, for cause and condition perish together. When the characteristics of the mind are all exhausted, it is called attaining *nirvāṇa* and accomplishing spontaneous activity (*anābhoga-karman*).

Next, the pure permeation (*viśuddha-vāsanā*) is explained. Within this, there are two parts: first the question, and then the answer. In the answer, there are also two parts: a brief explanation and a detailed exposition.
In the brief explanation, the permeation of *tathatā* is explained first, followed by the permeation of the deluded mind. Within this [latter], there are five sections.
The initial statement, "By means of this deluded mind... until one gains self-confidence in one's own nature," clarifies the faith within the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The subsequent statement, "Knowing that the movement of the mind is delusive and that no external objects exist, one cultivates the dharma of remoteness," reveals the cultivation within the stage of the Three Worthies (*tri-satkula*).
The phrase, "Because one knows as it truly is that no external objects exist," clarifies the first [stage].
The section from "In the stages" (*bhūmi*) up to "the realization of the path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*) concerns the perfection of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

The section from "various [dharmas]" (*nānāvidha*) down to "by the power of long-term habitual perfuming" (*dīrghakāla-vāsanā-vaśāt*) reveals the cultivation of the ten thousand practices (*sādhana*) during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The section from "ignorance is immediately extinguished" (*avidyā nirudhyate*) onwards, fifthly, reveals the realization of *nirvāṇa* at the stage of fruition (*phalabhūmi*).
The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are the two?

First is the perfuming of the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), which pertains to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who, weary of the suffering of birth and death, gradually advance toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities.
Second is the perfuming of the *manas* (the mental faculty), which refers to the bodhisattvas who, having generated courageous resolve, swiftly advance toward *nirvāṇa*.
Because of this revolving.
Next, in the detailed explanation, the delusive perfuming is clarified first. Regarding the "discriminative consciousness of phenomena" (*vikaḷpa-vijñāna*) therein:

speaking generally, all seven consciousnesses are termed the discriminative consciousness of phenomena; however, speaking according to their predominance, it refers specifically to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it performs discrimination.
It is used in its strong sense because it universally conditions all phenomena; therefore, this passage speaks according to that strong sense.
This consciousness does not know that all objects are merely consciousness, and thus it clings to the notion that there are truly existing realms external to the mind.

Although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles may incline toward practice, they still reckon that there is birth-and-death to be weary of and nirvana to be delighted in; this is no different from the discriminative *vastu-vijñāna*.

...this clinging. Therefore, it is called the "perfuming of the *vijñapti-vijñāna* (consciousness of discerning phenomena). As for the "perfuming of the *manas*," it is also called the "perfuming of the *karma-vijñāna*.
Generally speaking, all five types of consciousness are termed *manas*, as explained above in its meaning.

However, from the perspective of the fundamental source, only the *karma-vijñāna* is taken [as representative], because it is the most subtle and serves as the basis for all consciousnesses; therefore, within this context, the *karma-*...

Consciousness is called the *manas*. Thus, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) has not yet differentiated between the seeing and the perceived. However, the Bodhisattvas know that the mind is a false movement and that there are no separate objects;

they understand that all phenomena are merely the measure of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Having abandoned their previous attachment to external objects, they accord with the meaning of the karmic consciousness;

therefore, it is called the "perfuming of the karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna-vāsanā*), and is also termed the "perfuming of the *manas*. This does not mean that it is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) is that which is able to give rise to the mind and cultivate various practices.
Regarding the meaning of the permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā-vāsanā*), there are two kinds. What are these two? First, permeation by its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vāsanā*);

second, permeation through its functional activity (*vṛtti-vāsanā*). As for permeation by its own essential nature: from beginningless time, it has possessed uncontaminated dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and is fully endowed with them.
There is an inconceivable karma that constitutes the nature of its objective sphere.

Based on these two meanings, it constantly perfumes [the mind] and, by virtue of its power, enables sentient beings to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death, to joyfully seek nirvana, and to have self-confidence that their own bodies possess the *tathatā* (Suchness) dharma, thereby giving rise to the resolve to practice.
Question: If this is the meaning, then all sentient beings possess *tathatā*.
If all [beings] are equally permeated by [the seeds of] cultivation, why is it that some possess faith while others do not?

Why are there immeasurable distinctions between earlier and later states, such that they would all simultaneously realize for themselves the existence of the *tathatā* (True Suchness) dharma, diligently practice skillful means, and equally enter *nirvāṇa*? The answer is:

Although *tathatā* is fundamentally one, there are immeasurable and boundless instances of ignorance (*avidyā*). From the very beginning, these have possessed inherent differences in their nature, varying in degree of thickness and thinness.
Because they are identical. The various afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges arise from ignorance; the specific afflictions of self-view, craving, and attachment arise from ignorance.
All such afflictions arise based on ignorance, with infinite distinctions between preceding and succeeding states, which only a Tathāgata can know.
Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas have causes and conditions; [the cause is...]
When conditions are fully assembled, then accomplishment is achieved. For example, the nature of fire within wood is the direct cause of fire;

yet, if no one knows it and no skillful means are employed, it is impossible for it to burn the wood by itself. It is the same with sentient beings: although they possess the direct cause, [they cannot achieve liberation without conditions].
By the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), if one does not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and others as conditions,
it is impossible for one to spontaneously sever afflictions and enter *nirvāṇa*. Even if there is the power of external conditions,
if the internal pure dharmas lack the power of habitual perfuming, one will likewise be unable to ultimately weary of the suffering of birth and death or earnestly seek liberation.

Nirvāṇa. If the causes and conditions are complete—namely, by virtue of one's own power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), and because of the compassionate protection of the vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—one is able to give rise to a mind that loathes suffering and believes in the existence of Nirvāṇa.
One then cultivates roots of goodness. Because these cultivated roots of goodness reach maturity, one encounters the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provide instruction, benefit, and joy. Thereupon...
It is able to advance toward the path of nirvāṇa.
Within the permeation of true suchness (tathatā-vāsanā), there are three parts: first, the enumeration of the number as a general heading; second, the listing of the names according to that number.
Third is the clarification of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Within this clarification of characteristics, there are two parts: first, the individual explanation; second, the combined interpretation.
In the initial individual explanation, one first clarifies the permeation of the self-substance (*svabhāva*). Within this, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation;

second, the removal of doubts. Regarding the first, it says: "Possessing the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and being fully endowed with inconceivable karma" refers to the original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).

This is the gate of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*). That which acts as the nature of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is explained according to the objective sphere of the gate of emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*).
By relying on the power of this inherently existing object and wisdom, they secretly permeate the deluded mind, causing it to give rise to revulsion and joy, and so forth.

From the section beginning with "Question" below, the inquiry and response resolve doubts; the intent of the question is clear. Within the answer, there are two parts; the first concerns afflictions (*kleśa*).
The thickness and thinness [of these afflictions] clarify their inequality. Later, by citing their varying encounters with conditions, their inequality is further revealed.
Regarding the first point, the phrase "afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges" refers to ignorance regarding the phenomena of the various dharma-gates;
this is subsumed under the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The phrase "afflictions of self-view and attachment" refers to what is subsumed under the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The meaning of the response can be understood from this. Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Moreover, all Buddhas... onwards, it clarifies the variations in conditions (*pratyaya*). This consists of the dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis; the textual structure is evident.
That which functions as perfuming (*vāsanā*) is precisely the power of external conditions for sentient beings. Such external conditions possess immeasurable meanings.
Briefly stated, there are two kinds. What are the two? First, the differentiated condition; second, the equal condition. Regarding the differentiated condition:

from the time this person first resolves their mind and begins to seek the Way, until they attain Buddhahood, depending upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, they may see them or keep them in mind during that interval;
or [the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas] may act as their retinue, mothers, paternal relatives, or provide for them.

Whether acting as a friend, an enemy, or by employing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and so forth through all the immeasurable conditions of action, the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of great compassion enables sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness, for they obtain benefit through seeing or hearing [the Buddha].
These conditions are of two kinds. What are the two? First, the proximate condition (*āsanna-pratyaya*).

Because they attain deliverance quickly; second is the distant condition, because they attain deliverance after a long period. These two conditions—the proximate and the distant—are further divided into two types each.
What are these two? First is the condition for increasing practice; second is the condition for receiving the Way.
As for the universal condition, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally vow to deliver and liberate all sentient beings, naturally permeating them.
One practices this constantly and never abandons it. By virtue of the power of the wisdom of identical essence, one manifests karmic activities according to what is seen and heard as appropriate.
That is to say, sentient beings rely upon samādhi and thereby attain the equal vision of all Buddhas.
Within the section on "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), there are also three parts: a general heading, an enumeration of names, and a discernment of their characteristics.

Regarding the second part, the enumeration of names, the "differentiating conditions" (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*) act as conditions for the perfuming of the discriminative consciousness of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
As for those that can act as conditions, all from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward, up to the Buddhas, are capable of acting as conditions.
Furthermore, as for the "equal condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it serves as the condition for the karmic consciousness-habituation (*karma-vijñāna-vāsanā*) of all Bodhisattvas.

As for that which can act as the condition, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward through to the Buddhas, one must rely on the power of the wisdom of the same essence (*tathatā-svabhāva-jñāna-bala*) in order to function as the equal condition.
In the third section, the "Discrimination of Characteristics," the specific conditions (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*) are first clarified; therein are two parts, explained together.

Explanation. Within this explanation, there are also two parts. First, the opening of the two conditions of the proximate and the remote; second, the opening of the two conditions of practice and understanding. Regarding the condition for increasing practice:
it is so called because it can give rise to various practices such as generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*). Regarding the condition for entering the path:

it is so called because one enters the path by giving rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*). Within the condition of equality, there are two parts. First, the clarification of the enabling condition (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The phrase "as follows" explains the meaning of equality. Regarding those who perceive equality based on samādhi:

bodhisattvas from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward behold the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* with its immeasurable marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). These are all boundless and free from the characteristics of limitation;
therefore, it is said that they perceive all Buddhas as equal. If one is in a state of distracted mind, one cannot perceive [the Buddha] in such a manner.
These marks and signs are free from the characteristics of limitation; for this reason, it is said that they rely upon samādhi.
The preceding section has concluded the detailed explanation of the perfuming of essence and function.
This perfuming of essence and function is further divided into two types. What are these two? The first is that which is not yet in correspondence.

This refers to ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds. By means of the perfuming of the mind and mental consciousness, they are able to practice by relying on the power of faith.
Because they have not yet attained non-conceptual wisdom, they are not yet in correspondence with the essence (*tattva*).

Because they have not yet attained the practice of sovereign karma, they are not yet in correspondence with its function (*vṛtti*). "The two being in correspondence" refers to the dharma-body bodhisattvas, who have attained [non-conceptual wisdom].

The discriminating mind accords with the wisdom and function of all Buddhas; it practices spontaneously by relying solely on the power of the Dharma, for it perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness) and thereby extinguishes ignorance.

The second section explains the identity and function [of the storehouse consciousness]. This contains two parts: a general indication and a detailed explanation. Within the detailed explanation, first is the clarification of the state prior to mutual correspondence.

Regarding the phrase "the perfuming of the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness": for ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, this is termed the perfuming of the mental consciousness;

that is, the perfuming of the *vṛtti-vijñāna* (consciousness of phenomena). As for "Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds" and so forth: this refers to those from the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward.
The term "mental perfuming" (*manas-vāsanā*) refers to the meaning of the perfuming of the *karma-vijñāna*, as previously explained (in the *Bieji*).

Here, in contrast to those Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body who, upon realizing the Dharma-body, are free from the characteristic of the perceiving subject (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*), the Bodhisattvas prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) are said to possess mental perfuming;
this is because they still rely upon the *karma-vijñāna* and thus maintain the characteristic of the perceiving subject.

If one follows the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) regarding the meaning of seeing the Reward Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*), then from the stage of the Vajra [mind] downward, all possess the characteristics of being seen;
these are collectively termed the "karmic consciousness habituation" (*karma-vijñāna-vāsanā*), as will be explained below.
"Those who have not yet attained the non-conceptual mind in correspondence with its essence" means they have not yet attained correspondence with the essence of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas.

"Those who have not yet attained mastery in the correspondence between karma and function" means they have not yet attained correspondence with the functions of the two bodies—the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*—of the Buddhas.
Within those who have already attained such correspondence, there are the Bodhisattvas of the *dharmakāya*. Ten...
The Bodhisattva on the [eighth] stage attains non-conceptual mind because it accords with the essence.

It accords with the wisdom and activity of all Buddhas because it possesses the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*). It is "spontaneous practice" because from the eighth stage upward, there is no longer effortful application (*anābhoga*).
Within the fourth section of the fivefold analysis that further clarifies the causes through verbal expression, two types of perfuming (*vāsanā*) are specifically elucidated.
It remains as it was before.
Furthermore, defiled dharmas have been perfuming [the mind] uninterruptedly since beginningless time; this continues until the attainment of Buddhahood, after which they are severed.
However, the perfuming of pure dharmas is never severed, persisting until the end of the future. What is the meaning of this? It is because of True Suchness (tathatā).

Because the Dharma constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharmakāya manifests. Because it gives rise to the perfuming of the arising of function, there is no interruption.
Below this, the fifth section clarifies the meaning of the two kinds of perfuming being exhausted or not exhausted. It seeks to clarify that defiled perfuming contradicts principle, yet...
Because they arise, there is cessation; the permeation of pure dharmas arises in accordance with principle. Because it accords with principle, there is no cessation.
The meaning of the text is clear.
Within the section explaining the correct meaning (*samyagartha-vibhāga*), there are two major parts. The first is the explanation of the chapter on dharmas (*dharma-pada*).
The section on the gates concludes above.
