△ Below this is the second section, the Chapter on Explaining the Meaning. In the preceding section on establishing the doctrine, two kinds of meaning were set forth:

namely, the meaning of "Greatness" (mahatva) and the meaning of "Vehicle" (yāna). In this present text, the meaning of "Greatness" is primarily explained, while the meaning of "Vehicle" is incidentally revealed.

This section contains two parts: first, a general explanation of the essence and characteristics of the two types of Greatness; second, a detailed analysis of the meaning of the Greatness of Function (vṛtti-mahatva).
Furthermore, as for the essential nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*): it neither increases nor decreases across all ordinary beings, *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas.
It is not born in the past limit, nor does it perish in the future limit; it is ultimately eternal and constant, having been so from the very beginning.
The nature itself is inherently replete with all meritorious virtues. This is because its essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light;
the meaning of universally illuminating the dharma-realm; the meaning of true and authentic cognition; the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind;
the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty. It is endowed with such virtues that exceed those of the Ganges River.
The sands are not separate from, not severed from, and not different from the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas;
because they fulfill them completely without deficiency, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and is also called the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*. Question:
It was stated above that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is equal and free from all marks. Why, then, is it further said that its essence possesses such various merits? Answer:

It is said: "Although these various meanings of merit truly exist, they possess no marks of differentiation; they are equal in a single flavor, being nothing other than True Suchness (tathatā). How is this so?
Because it is non-discriminative and free from the marks of discrimination, there is thus no duality. Furthermore, by what meaning can differentiation be spoken of?
It is shown by relying on the arising and ceasing marks of the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna). How is this shown? By... [text continues]

All phenomena are fundamentally mind-only. In reality, there is no thought, yet there is a deluded mind; failing to realize this, it gives rise to thoughts and perceives various objective realms, which is why it is called ignorance.
When the nature of the mind does not arise, this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.
If the mind gives rise to views, there is the characteristic of non-seeing. Because the nature of the mind is free from views, it is the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.
If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition; it lacks intrinsic nature, and is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure.
Subject to feverish affliction and decay, it is not sovereign, and so forth, possessing as many defilements of delusion as there are sands in the Ganges.

Regarding this meaning: because the nature of the mind is unmoving in relation to this meaning, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of all pure merits, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If the mind were to arise and perceive any further phenomena as objects of recollection, it would be deficient.
Such immeasurable merits of pure dharmas are themselves the one mind; there is nothing further to be recollected. Therefore, it is complete and is called [the Tathāgatagarbha].
It is the treasury of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.

Regarding the initial statement concerning its "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), this is a general restatement of the meanings of the greatness of essence (*dharmatā-mahattva*) and the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*).
The subsequent statement that it is eternally and ultimately constant, without increase or decrease, from all ordinary beings up to all Buddhas, is the explanation of the essence.

"Great. In the preceding establishment of the thesis, it was stated that "one" refers to the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*), meaning that the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is equal, without increase or decrease.
The subsequent passage, beginning with "from the very beginning, its nature is spontaneously fulfilled," explains the meaning of the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*).

The preceding statement regarding the "two" refers to the magnitude of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*), meaning that the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmatā-guṇa*).

Within this passage, there are two parts: first, a direct elucidation of the characteristics of the qualities of nature; second, a further clarification through a series of questions and answers as to why this is so.
The intent of the question is clear. The response consists of two parts: a general answer and a detailed exposition. Within the detailed exposition, there are two further sections:

first, clarifying the meaning of non-duality within differentiation; second, clarifying the meaning of differentiation within non-duality. This latter section also has two parts: a brief indication and [a detailed explanation].

Broad explanation: Regarding the brief indication that states, "By means of the marks of arising and ceasing of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), [the Tathāgata] manifests," it is because within these marks of arising and ceasing there are various faults and afflictions;
yet, by citing their source, it is called "karmic consciousness. In contrast to these various defects, the various merits are explained. As for the phrase "How is this manifested?
and so forth, it specifically addresses various faults to reveal the meaning of the virtues; the textual structure may be understood accordingly.
[Understood.
△ Below is the second section, the detailed explanation of the meaning of the "Great Function" (*mahā-vṛtti*). This contains two parts: a general clarification and a detailed explanation.

Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it refers to how the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, while originally on the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), give rise to great compassion.
They cultivate the various pāramitās, gather and transform sentient beings, and establish great vows, desiring to deliver and liberate all within the realm of sentient beings without exception;
they do not limit themselves by the number of kalpas, but continue until the end of the future, because they regard all sentient beings as their own bodies.
Furthermore, one does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings. By what meaning is this so?
It means that one knows all sentient beings and one’s own body as they truly are—equal in *tathatā* (suchness) and without distinction.

Because there is such great wisdom of skillful means, ignorance is eradicated and the fundamental *dharmakāya* is seen. Thereupon, inconceivable activities and various functions arise spontaneously. That is to say:
It is equal to True Suchness (tathatā) and pervades all places; furthermore, no characteristic of functional activity can be apprehended therein.
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the body of the Dharma-body characterized by wisdom, which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

It has no sphere of worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and is free from deliberate activity; it is only said to have "function" insofar as sentient beings obtain benefit through seeing and hearing it according to their own perceptions.
The beginning and middle also consist of two parts: first, citing the cause in relation to the fruit; second, restating the cause to reveal the fruit.

Within the initial citation of the cause, there are also three phrases: first, the practice; second, the vow; and third, the clarification of skillful means. The initial statement, "The Buddhas originally, while on the ground of causal practice...
[until] gathering and transforming sentient beings," cites their original practice. Next, the statement, "They established great vows... [and so forth].
"Reaching to the end of the future" refers to the original vow.

Next, the statement "by means of grasping sentient beings up to the equality of *tathatā*" refers to wisdom, compassion, and great skillful means. From "by means of" onwards, the second section reveals the fruit;
herein there are also three parts. First, the phrase "because one possesses such great skillful means and wisdom" restates the preceding cause.
Furthermore, the subsequent statement, "extinguishing ignorance and perceiving the fundamental Dharmakāya," refers to the fruit of self-benefit.
From the words "spontaneously" (*svayam*) onwards, it correctly reveals the characteristics of its activity (*vṛtti-lakṣaṇa*). Within this, there are three phrases.

The first, stating "the inconceivable activity of various functions," clarifies that the activity is profoundly deep. The second, stating "it is equal to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and pervades all places," reveals...
This is because its functioning is vast and great. Furthermore, the following passage clarifies that it functions through non-characteristic (*animitta*) while responding to conditions (*pratyaya*).

This is what is meant by the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: "For example, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*maṇi*) or a celestial drum (*devadundubhi*), they accomplish their own tasks without thought. This concludes the general explanation of its functioning.

This function is of two kinds. What are these two? First, that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects), is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).
Because they do not know that it is manifested by the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses), they perceive it as coming from the outside;
they grasp at its physical dimensions and cannot know it exhaustively. Second, that which is based on the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness) refers to all Bodhisattvas from the beginning...
That which is perceived by the mind from the initial aspiration up to the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva is called the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

This body possesses immeasurable colors; these colors possess immeasurable marks; these marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics; and the resultant environment upon which it rests is likewise immeasurable.
These various adornments, manifesting according to what is shown, are boundless and inexhaustible;
they transcend all marks of limitation and, as appropriate, can always be maintained, neither destroyed nor lost.
Such merits are all accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices of the *pāramitās* and the inconceivable permeation, and are fully endowed with the immeasurable.
Because it possesses the characteristic of bliss, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Furthermore, that which is seen by ordinary beings is its coarse form;

as they are seen differently according to the six realms of existence, appearing in various distinct categories, it does not possess the characteristic of experiencing bliss, and is therefore called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body).

Moreover, that which is seen by Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment] and others is [the Enjoyment Body], because they have deep faith in the *tathatā* (Suchness) Dharma, though only to a limited degree.

He sees and knows that the adornments of those forms and other such matters neither come nor go; they are free from spatial limits and appear solely in dependence upon the mind, never departing from True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Nevertheless, this bodhisattva still engages in conceptual discrimination because he has not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
If one attains a pure mind, what is perceived becomes subtle and its function becomes increasingly superior, until reaching the ultimate vision at the end of the Bodhisattva stages.
If one is separated from the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), there is no appearance of seeing;
for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas possesses no such mutual perception of color-forms or characteristics. Question: If the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are devoid of color-forms, how can they...
Question: How does it manifest material forms? Answer: Because this very *dharmakāya* is the substance of form, it is able to manifest form.

That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual. Since the nature of form is itself wisdom (*jñāna*), the substance of form is formless and is called the "wisdom-body" (*jñānakāya*).
Since the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) that pervades all places. As for the forms manifested, they are without...
There are limits [to the physical world], yet according to the mind, one can manifest the worlds of the ten directions, with immeasurable bodhisattvas, immeasurable reward bodies (*vipākakāya*),
and immeasurable adornments, each distinct and differentiated, all without limit and yet not obstructing one another.
This cannot be known through the discrimination of consciousness, for it is due to the principle of the sovereign function of *tathatā*.
The second part is the detailed explanation. This consists of three sections: the general heading, the detailed exposition, and the exchange for resolving doubts.

Within the detailed exposition, there are also two parts: first, the direct manifestation of specific functions; second, the restatement and further analysis. In the first of these, there are likewise two sub-sections.

First, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is clarified; subsequently, the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is revealed. Regarding the initial statement, "based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects)":

ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not yet know that all is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). They falsely reckon that external objects exist; this is precisely the meaning of the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*.

Now, when seeing the Buddha-body, they likewise reckon it to be outside the mind, which accords with the meaning of the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness). Therefore, it is said that one sees based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*.
This person does not know that the appearance of forms is manifested based on their own evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Therefore, they say that because they do not know it is the evolving consciousness that manifests them, the vision comes from the outside. However, what they perceive consists of delimited forms; these are actually without limit and free from the characteristic of delimitation.
That person merely grasps the aspect of being delimited, failing to understand that what is delimited is in fact without limit. Thus...
This is because one cannot fully know the limits of what is grasped as form. Regarding the statement that within the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) one "relies upon the *karmavijñāna*":
Bodhisattvas from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) upward are able to understand that there is only mind and no external objects;

they perceive the Buddha-body in accordance with the principle of the *karmavijñāna*. Therefore, it is said that they see by relying on the *karmavijñāna*. However, these Bodhisattvas know its limitations.
Since equality is itself without limits, it is said that whatever is manifested is likewise boundless, even unto its indestructibility and non-loss.
These unimpeded and inconceivable matters all arise from the permeation of the profound practice of the six perfections.
Furthermore, it is accomplished through the inconceivable perfuming of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Based on this meaning, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).

Therefore, it is said that it is termed "enjoyment" because it is fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss. However, regarding these two bodies, there are differing explanations in the sūtras and śāstras.
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* states that attaining Buddhahood in a defiled land is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body), while in a pure land...

The attainment of enlightenment is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body). The *Suvarṇabhāsottama-sūtra* states that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
The body manifested according to the characteristics of the six realms of existence is called the *nirmāṇakāya*.
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, that which is seen prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is called the *nirmāṇakāya*, while that which is seen from the stages onward is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. Now...
In this treatise, the differentiated marks of the six realms as perceived by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
That which is seen by bodhisattvas of the ten stages of understanding and above—free from the limitations of form—is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body).

The reason for such differences is that the gateways to the Dharma are immeasurable and do not follow a single path; therefore, whatever is established according to these circumstances is all [valid].
There is a logical principle. Therefore, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is taught that what is seen by the distracted mind prior [to meditative concentration] possesses delimited characteristics;
thus, it belongs to the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body). In this present treatise, however, it is clarified that what is seen by the bodhisattva’s samādhi is free from delimited characteristics;
thus, it belongs to the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body). By this reasoning, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, as for what is seen by ordinary beings...
Below this, the second section restates and analyzes [the text]. First, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is clarified; the textual structure is easily understood.

Next, from "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) onwards, the characteristics of the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) are revealed. This contains two parts: first, what is seen by those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*); second, what is seen by those on the stages.
Regarding the first of these, the statement "because of deep faith in the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, one sees it partially" is as follows: ten... [etc. (as in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*).
Regarding "understanding within": relying on the gate of the emptiness of persons to perceive the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) constitutes a semblance understanding;

therefore, it is called "partial. The passage from "if one attains the pure mind" onwards reveals what is perceived on the stages (*bhūmi*). As for the statement "if one is free from the *karmic consciousness*, there is no aspect of seeing":

it is only by depending upon the *karmic consciousness* that there exist the evolving aspect (*vivartana-lakṣaṇa*) and the manifesting aspect (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, if one is free from the *karmic consciousness*, these are absent.
This is the section on "Observing the Characteristics. The questions and answers that follow resolve doubts; the structure of the text is clear.
Within the exposition of the correct meaning, there are two major divisions. The first, the formal explanation of the established doctrine, has already been concluded above.
Furthermore, this demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) directly from the gate of Arising and Ceasing.

This refers to investigating the five aggregates (*skandhas*), both matter and mind, and the objects of the six sense-fields, which are ultimately devoid of thought. Because the mind has no form or characteristics, it cannot be found even if sought throughout the ten directions;
it is like a person who, due to delusion, mistakes the east for the west, while the directions themselves have not actually shifted. Sentient beings are just like this.

Due to the delusion of ignorance, one takes the mind to be thought; yet the mind is in reality unmoving. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one will immediately attain compliance with and entry into the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).

The second section reveals the gateway for entering the ultimate meaning through the medium of the provisional. It contains three parts: a general heading, a detailed explanation, and a third concluding summary.
Within the general heading, the phrase "investigating the five aggregates, both form and mind," refers to the aggregate of form as "form" (rūpa).

The remaining four are called "mind. Within the detailed explanation, the contemplation of form (*rūpa*) is explained first: one breaks down all forms down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), until they can no longer be apprehended.
Apart from the mind, there is no characteristic that can be conceptualized; therefore, it is said that the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are ultimately without conceptualization.
It is not only that there are no separate form-objects outside the mind; even when seeking form within the mind, it cannot be found.
Therefore, it is said that the mind has no form or characteristics; one may seek it throughout the ten directions, yet it can never be found.
From "As follows" below, we next contemplate the dharma of the mind. First is the analogy, followed by the application (*yōjō*).

Within the application, the statement that "the mind is truly unmoving" means that when one investigates the movement of thought, it is found to have already ceased or not yet arisen, with nothing abiding in between. Because there is nothing that abides, there is no arising. Thus one knows.
The nature of the mind is truly immovable. From "If one is able to... onwards is the third section, the summary.
"Attaining compliance" refers to expedient contemplation; "entering the gate of True Suchness" refers to correct contemplation.
△ Second, the antidote to false attachments. This section also consists of four parts: first, a general statement enumerating the number; second, listing the names according to that number;
third, defining the characteristics according to those names; and fourth, a general demonstration of the ultimate departure from attachment.
Regarding the antidote to false attachments: all false attachments depend upon the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). If one is free from the self, there are no false attachments.
This view of a self is of two kinds.
First, the number is stated in general.
What are the two? First, the view of a self of persons (*pudgala-ātman-dṛṣṭi*); second, the view of a self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the mention of "the view of a self of persons" in the second section, which enumerates the names, it refers to the conceptualization of a sovereign entity possessing a general characteristic. This is called...

Regarding the grasping at a self of persons (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*) and the view of a self of phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*): the former calculates that all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is called the grasping at phenomena.

The grasping at phenomena is that which arises in the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Herein, the grasping at a person refers specifically to that which arises among those within the Buddha's teachings who are beginners in the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the view of self and person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), it is said that there are five types based on the teachings for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). What are these five?

First, having heard the *sūtras* state that the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is ultimately quiescent and like empty space, because they do not understand this as being for the purpose of destroying attachment, they claim that empty space itself is the nature of the Tathāgata.
How is this to be countered? It is by clarifying that the characteristics of empty space are its...
Delusory phenomena have no real substance; they exist only in relation to form and possess the characteristic of being visible, causing the mind to arise and perish.
Since all phenomena of form are fundamentally the mind, there is in reality no external form. If there were no external form, then even the characteristic of empty space would not exist.
Thus, all objective realms exist only because the deluded mind arises. If the mind is free from delusion...
When movement ceases, all objective realms are extinguished, and the single true mind alone is omnipresent.
This is called the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast intrinsic wisdom; it is not like the characteristics of empty space. Second, as it is said in the Sūtras:
All phenomena in the world are ultimately empty in essence; even the dharmas of nirvāṇa and suchness are ultimately empty.
They have been empty from the very beginning and are devoid of all marks. Because [sentient beings] do not understand this, they fall into attachment;
thus, they claim that the nature of suchness and nirvāṇa is merely emptiness. How is this countered? By clarifying the self-substance of the dharma-body of suchness.
It is not empty, for it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic qualities (*dharmas*). Third, regarding what is heard in the *sūtras*:
it is said that the Tathāgata-garbha neither increases nor decreases, and its essence is complete with all dharmas of merit.

Because of a lack of understanding, one might claim that the Tathāgata-garbha possesses the distinct characteristics of material and mental phenomena (*rūpa-citta-dharma*). How is this countered? It is by relying solely upon True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because it is explained according to its meaning. It is because the distinctions are manifested through the teaching on the sense of arising, ceasing, and defilement.

Fourth, when hearing the Sūtra state that all worldly phenomena of birth and death and all defiled dharmas exist in dependence upon the Tathāgatagarbha, and that all dharmas do not depart from True Suchness (tathatā), yet due to a lack of understanding, one claims that the self-essence of the Tathāgatagarbha inherently possesses all worldly phenomena.

Regarding phenomena such as birth and death, how are they counteracted? It is because the Tathāgatagarbha, from the very beginning, possesses only pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable from, uninterrupted by, and non-different from the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā).

Furthermore, the defiled phenomena of afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges exist only as delusions; their nature is inherently non-existent from the start, having never existed since beginningless time.
Because it is associated with the *tathāgatagarbha*, if the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* possessed deluded phenomena such that its realization would cause those delusions to cease forever,

such a thing would be impossible. Fifth, upon hearing the *sūtras* state that birth and death exist based on the *tathāgatagarbha* and that nirvāṇa is attained based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, because they do not understand this, they claim that sentient beings have a beginning.
Because they perceive a beginning, they further claim that the nirvāṇa attained by the Tathāgata has an end, and that he returns to becoming a sentient being.
How is this countered? Because the tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit, the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning.
If one were to say that there are sentient beings who first arise outside of the three realms, this would be the teaching of the non-Buddhist scriptures.
Furthermore, the tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit; since the nirvāṇa attained by all Buddhas is in correspondence with it, it likewise has no posterior limit.
In the third section, the clarification of characteristics, the view of a personal self (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) is first explained. This consists of two parts: a general heading and a detailed exposition.
Within the detailed exposition, five types are specifically revealed, each containing three phrases. The first [phrase] sets forth the cause for the arising of the view;
the second clarifies the nature of the attachment; and the last reveals the antidote. Regarding the first type of attachment, the statement "space itself is the nature of the Tathāgata" means:
It should be understood that the nature of the Tathāgata is identical to the characteristic of empty space.

Regarding the second point, which states that even the dharma of *nirvāṇa* and *tathatā* is ultimately empty: as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "Even *nirvāṇa* is like an illusion and like a dream.
If there were any dharma superior to *nirvāṇa*, I would say that it, too, is like an illusion and like a dream. Thus, the second...
Regarding the manifestation of the meanings of cause, arising, ceasing, and defilement within the [first] three [categories], it is as stated in the aforementioned text:

"By relying on the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the karmic consciousness," and so forth, as explained at length. Regarding the statement in the fourth [category] that they are "not separate" and "not interrupted," etc.:
This is as explained in detail in the *Commentary on Neither Increasing nor Decreasing*.

Regarding the fifth point, the statement that "if one says there are sentient beings outside the three realms who first arise, this is the teaching of non-Buddhist scriptures," is because it is as stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.
Thus far, these five attachments all rely upon the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgatagarbha, and so forth, as the universal subject.
Because they give rise to such attachments, it is collectively termed "attachment to a person" (*pudgala-grāha*).
As for the "view of a self in phenomena" (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), because the two vehicles possess dull faculties, the Tathāgata taught them only the non-self of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Since that teaching was not ultimate, they perceived the five aggregates as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, fearing birth and death, they falsely grasped at *nirvāṇa*. Why?
What is the antidote? Because the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) do not arise by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*), they do not cease;
they are primordially in *nirvāṇa*. Within the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*), there are likewise three points: first, clarifying the cause for the arising of the view;
second, below the section on "seeing," manifesting the characteristics of grasping; and third, from "how" onwards, manifesting its antidote. The textual structure is clear.
Furthermore, for one who has ultimately abandoned false attachments, it should be known that defiled phenomena and pure phenomena are entirely mutually dependent;

they possess no intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) that can be described. Therefore, all phenomena from the very beginning have neither form nor mind, neither wisdom nor consciousness, and are neither existent nor non-existent.
Their characteristics are ultimately ineffable. As for those who nevertheless employ verbal expressions, it should be known that [they do so] by means of the Tathāgata’s...

Through skillful means, they provisionally employ verbal teachings to guide sentient beings. Their underlying intent is for all to transcend conceptual thought and return to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is because conceiving of all dharmas causes the mind to undergo birth and extinction, thereby preventing entry into true wisdom.
The fourth section concerns the meaning of ultimate freedom from grasping. This contains two parts: first, clarifying the principle that all phenomena transcend verbal expression;
second, revealing the intent behind the provisional use of verbal teachings. The textual structure is clear.
△ In the third section, "The Section on Setting Out," there are two parts: first, a general statement of the main intent; second, a detailed classification and analysis.
Regarding the analysis of the characteristics of the path of setting out: it refers to the path realized by all Buddhas and [the path of] all Bodhisattvas.

Because the purpose is to proceed toward the practice of generating the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), the initial statement regarding "the path realized by all Buddhas" identifies the path toward which one proceeds.

The subsequent section, beginning with "all bodhisattvas," clarifies the conduct capable of proceeding thereon; this is intended to elucidate the bodhisattva’s generation of the resolve and its directed application.
This is the path realized by the Buddha; therefore, it is called "the characteristics of the path of differentiation and progression.
△ Below is the second section, the detailed classification, which contains three parts: first, stating the number and opening the chapters;
second, listing the names according to that number; and third, defining the characteristics according to those names.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). What are these three? First, the generation of the mind through the perfection of faith;
second, the generation of the mind through practice based on understanding; and third, the generation of the mind through realization.

The first part of the text is clear. Regarding the second section, the statement "the mind generated through the accomplishment of faith" refers to the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), which also includes the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Within the stage of the Ten Faiths, one cultivates the mind of faith; once this faith is accomplished, one generates the mind of resolve (*niścaya-citta*).
One immediately enters the ten stages (*bhūmi*); therefore, this is called "the arousal of the mind through the accomplishment of faith.

As for "the arousal of the mind through practice based on understanding," it occurs during the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), while also incorporating the ten practices (*caryā*). Within the stage of the ten practices, one is able to understand the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and accord with the *dharmadhātu*.

Having cultivated the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) until they are mature, one arouses the mind of dedication and enters the stage of dedication; hence, it is termed "practice based on understanding."
Regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*): the "realized arousal of the mind" refers to the stages from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward through the tenth ground.
Based on the two preceding types of similar arousal of the mind, one realizes the true mind of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
△ Third, the analysis of characteristics. This section contains three parts, as the three types of mind are explained in sequence as previously stated.
△ Within the first, the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*), there are likewise three parts: 1. the practice for accomplishing clear faith; 2.
the manifestation of the characteristics of generating the mind through the accomplishment of practice; and 3. the praise of the merits obtained by generating the mind.

Regarding those who have achieved faith and resolve their aspiration for enlightenment: upon what kind of person does this depend? What practices must they cultivate to achieve the perfection of faith and become capable of generating the aspiration?
It is said that it depends on sentient beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).

Because they possess the power of cultivated roots of goodness, they believe in the retribution of karma, are able to give rise to the ten wholesome actions, and, weary of the suffering of birth and death, desire to seek unsurpassed bodhi. Having encountered various Buddhas, they personally...

Having received offerings and practiced the cultivation of faith for ten thousand kalpas, because that faith has been perfected, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Alternatively, out of great compassion, they are able to resolve their own minds;

or, when the True Dharma is about to perish, they are able to resolve their own minds through the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma. Those who have thus resolved their minds through the perfection of faith enter into the correct [Path].
The group of those destined for certainty (niyata-rāśi) never regresses; they are said to dwell within the lineage of the Tathāgata, being in accord with the true cause.

If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha and receive offerings from him, [they do not attain such certainty].

Nevertheless, they may plant the seeds for rebirth as humans or devas, or plant the seeds for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Even among those who seek the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), their faculties are not fixed;

they may advance or regress. Some, having made offerings to various Buddhas for less than ten thousand *kalpas*, may nevertheless give rise to the resolve [for enlightenment] upon encountering certain conditions—namely, by beholding the physical marks and features of a Buddha, or perhaps through making offerings to the Saṅgha.
A monk may resolve his mind [on enlightenment] either because he is exhorted by those of the Two Vehicles to do so, or because he emulates others in resolving his mind.
Such resolutions of the mind are entirely uncertain; encountering adverse conditions, they may suddenly regress and fall to the level of the Two Vehicles.

The beginning and middle also consist of two parts: first the question, and then the answer. Within the question, the phrase "relying upon what kind of person" asks about the person capable of cultivation;
"practicing what kind of conduct" asks about the conduct that is cultivated;

and "attaining the fulfillment of faith and being capable of generating the resolve" asks regarding the accomplishment of that conduct in relation to the fruit of generating the resolve. Within the answer, there are two parts. First:
This provides the direct answer to the question. Second, it reveals the superior by contrasting it with the inferior.

Within this direct answer, in response to the first three questions, the initial statement regarding "sentient beings of the indeterminate group" answers the first question by identifying those capable of cultivation.

While there are many ways to distinguish the three groups, the present text directly clarifies that from the stage of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vyākaraṇa*) upward, [the bodhisattvas] are determined.

Those who do not regress are called the group of right certainty (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*). Those who have not yet entered the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and do not believe in cause and effect are called the group of wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).

Between these two, those who are tending toward the Path, having resolved their minds to seek unsurpassed bodhi but whose resolve is not yet firm—sometimes advancing and sometimes regressing—are called the ten stages of faith;
they are termed the group of no fixed certainty (*aniyata-rāśi*). Now, based on such persons, I shall clarify that which is practiced.
[This is] practice. From "there is the power of perfumed roots of goodness" onwards, the second question is answered in turn, clarifying the practice cultivated by those of indeterminate nature.

Regarding the phrase "the power of perfumed roots of goodness": it refers to practicing such acts as faith because one relies on the internal power of perfuming within the *tathāgatagarbha* and further relies on the power of roots of goodness cultivated in previous lives. Regarding the phrase "faith in the fruits of karma": [it means...]
"Those whose retribution enables them to give rise to the ten wholesome acts" refers to giving rise to the wholesome roots of the merit portion (*puṇyabhāga*).
"Those who weary of the suffering of birth and death and seek the unsurpassed path" refers to generating the mind of the path portion (*mārgabhāga*).

"Those who encounter the various Buddhas and practice with confidence" correctly clarifies the cultivation of the wholesome roots of the path portion, namely, the cultivation of the ten kinds of confidence; their characteristics are fully detailed in the "Chapter on the One Path."
It is said: "After ten thousand kalpas have passed," which answers the third question and clarifies the characteristics of the accomplishment of faith.
This section contains two parts: first, citing the duration of time to clarify the conditions for accomplishing the arousal of the mind;
second, defining the assembly to reveal the stage in which that arousal of the mind resides. Regarding the first, it says that the confidence [of faith] reaches ten thousand kalpas.
"Accomplishment" refers to the accomplishment of faith after ten thousand kalpas within the stage of the Ten Faiths; one then enters the Ten Abidings.

As the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Vows) states: "This Bodhisattva of Faith-Imagination practices the ten precepts for ten thousand kalpas and shall enter the mind of the Ten Abidings, entering the position of the first abiding.
The commentary explains that the "position of the first abiding" entered here refers to...
The first stage of the Ten Abidings is the Stage of Initial Aspiration for Enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*). In this stage, one finally attains non-retrogressive faith;
therefore, it is also called "entering the ten minds through faith. This does not refer to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) prior to the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vyākhyāna*).

How is this known to be so? As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) states: "The lineage of cultivated seeds (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*) possesses ten minds, which have already transcended all the virtues of the two vehicles."

Regarding the stage of "Patience in Practice" (śikṣā-kṣānti): Bodhisattvas who have previously practiced the ten wholesome paths within this stage may regress or advance, just as light feathers are driven east and west by the wind.
Even if they practice the ten right paths for ten thousand kalpas and resolve upon bodhicitta, it is only then that they enter the stage of Patience in Practice.
This is known through the scriptural evidence; when the Sūtra speaks of "ten thousand," it refers to this very same [period].

"Ten thousand. Regarding the statement that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct [beings] to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and so forth: there are many conditions for arousing this aspiration;
here, we briefly set forth three types of superior conditions. From "In this way" onwards, it reveals the stages (*bhūmi*) in which the arousal of the aspiration resides.
The phrase "from the accomplishment of faith until entering the stage of right determination" refers to entering the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*).
Because of this, it is said that they are ultimately non-retrogressive. At that moment, they are precisely in the stage of the "nature of practice" (*śikṣāgotra*);
therefore, it is said that they are "dwelling within the lineage of the Tathāgata. Their practice accords with the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Therefore, it is also said that they correspond with the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*). The foregoing constitutes the formal response to the first three questions.

From the passage beginning "If there are... onwards, the inferior is cited to manifest the superior. Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), there are both superior and inferior types. The superior ones proceed as previously described into the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*);
the inferior ones fall back in this manner into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*). As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "All bodhisattvas..."
While the Bodhisattva is within the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), his cultivation of the Mahāyāna is not yet firm;

he feels much aversion and fear toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and his mind of compassion for sentient beings remains weak and thin. He thus desires to abandon the original vow of the Mahāyāna and cultivate the path of the Hīnayāna;

hence it is said that he "desires to practice the Hīnayāna. The general meaning is as stated above, and the textual details are clear. Thus far, the clarification of the accomplishment of faith has been explained.
Practice.
Furthermore, regarding the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith: what kind of mind is aroused? Briefly stated, there are three types. What are these three?

First is the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of suchness (*tathatā*). Second is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because it delights in gathering all [virtues].
Because of virtuous conduct. Third is the mind of great compassion, because one desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings. Question:

Since it was previously taught that the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic and the essence of the Buddha is non-dual, why does one not simply contemplate True Suchness alone, but must further seek to learn various virtuous practices?
Answer: It is like a great maṇi jewel; its essential nature is luminous and pure, yet it may be covered by mineral impurities.
Stain. Just as a person may contemplate the nature of a jewel, yet if they do not employ various skillful means to grind and polish it, it will never become pure;
likewise, the *dharmatā* of the *tathatā* of sentient beings is by nature empty and pure, yet it is defiled by immeasurable afflictions.
Even if a person contemplates *tathatā*, if they do not cultivate it through various skillful means, it likewise cannot become pure, because the stains [are present].
Because [the] measure pervades all phenomena, one cultivates all wholesome practices as an antidote.
If a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they will naturally accord with the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness). Briefly stated, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).
What are the four? First is the skillful means of the root of practice, which refers to contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen and free from...
Deluded views. Not abiding in saṃsāra, one contemplates that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and that the fruits of karma are never lost.

Giving rise to great compassion, one cultivates various merits to gather and transform sentient beings. Not abiding in nirvāṇa, this is because one accords with the non-abiding nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Second is the skillful means of cessation, which refers to shame, remorse, and repentance; these can cease all unwholesome dharmas.

It causes them to increase, because by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is free from all faults. Third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*):
namely, diligently making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem, praising and rejoicing in their merits, and entreating the Buddhas.
Because of a heart of profound love and reverence for the Triple Gem, faith increases, whereby one is able to aspire to the unsurpassed path. Furthermore...
Because they are protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they are able to eliminate karmic obstructions and their roots of goodness do not regress;

this is because they accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and are free from the obstruction of delusion. Fourth is the skillful means of great vows of equality, which refers to making the vow to exhaust the future, transforming and delivering all sentient beings without exception, causing them all to ultimately attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder. By...
Because it accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without interruption, the nature of phenomena is vast and pervasive, encompassing all sentient beings.
It is equal and non-dual, without thoughts of self or other, for it is ultimately quiescent.

The second [section] clarifies the characteristics of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*). Within this, there are two parts: first, a direct explanation; second, a dialectical discussion to dispel doubts.
Regarding the first, "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) means the sense of being non-crooked. If one contemplates *tathatā* (suchness), the mind is equanimous and free from any further divergence;
how could there be any crookedness? Therefore, it is said: "Because of correctly contemplating the dharma of *tathatā*. This is precisely...
These two are the root of all practices. As for "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*), it signifies the meaning of reaching the ultimate source.
If even a single good deed is lacking, there is no way to return to that source. The fulfillment of returning to the source necessarily requires the possession of myriad practices;

therefore, it is said that one "delights in accumulating all virtuous deeds. This is the foundation of practices for one's own benefit. As for "great compassionate mind" (*mahākaruṇā*), it signifies the meaning of universal salvation.
Therefore, it is said that one desires to uproot the suffering of sentient beings; this is the very foundation of altruistic practice.
When these three minds are generated, there is no evil from which one does not distance oneself, no virtue that one does not cultivate, and not a single sentient being who is not liberated.
This is called the unsurpassed bodhicitta. The questions and answers that follow clarify doubts; the intent of the questions is evident, while the answers [are as follows].

There are two [parts]: the direct answer and the further elucidation. Within the initial direct answer, there is the simile and the application; from "briefly stated" onwards, the further elucidation may be understood.
Because the bodhisattva has given rise to this mind, they obtain a partial vision of the dharmakāya.

By virtue of seeing the dharmakāya, they are able to manifest eight ways of benefiting sentient beings according to their power of aspiration; namely: descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, and so forth.

Whether dwelling in the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving the household life, attaining the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, or entering nirvana—yet this bodhisattva is not yet called the Dharmakāya.
This is because, throughout immeasurable past lives, their out-flowing (sāsrava) karma has not been definitively severed;
thus, they remain subject to slight suffering in accordance with their place of birth. Nevertheless, they are not bound by karma, for they possess the sovereign power of their great vows.
As stated in the sūtras, there are instances where it is said that some fall back and descend into the evil destinies; however, this is not an actual falling back.
It is merely for the sake of instilling courage in those beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and might become indolent.

Furthermore, once a bodhisattva has first resolved their mind, they remain far removed from timidity and ultimately never fear falling into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). If they hear...
For immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they attain *nirvāṇa* through diligent practice of difficult austerities, yet they do not become disheartened,
for through faith they know that all phenomena have been *nirvāṇa* from the very beginning.

The third section reveals the merit of generating the bodhicitta; it contains four parts: first, the manifestation of superior merit; second, the clarification of subtle faults; third, the accommodation of provisional teachings;

and fourth, the praise of those who practice according to reality. Within the first part, the initial two phrases—“those who have attained a partial vision of the Dharmakāya”—clarify the merit of self-benefit.
This refers to Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Understandings (*daśa-avabodha*), who, by relying on the gateway of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), perceive the Dharma...
The realms are seen as being similar; therefore, it is said they are "partial. From the phrase "according to the power of their vows" onwards, the virtue of benefiting others is revealed.

Regarding the ability to manifest eight kinds of ways to benefit sentient beings, it is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* when praising the first stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*):
"This bodhisattva who has generated the resolve attains the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies, all within a single..."
This is because he manifests the attainment of Buddhahood for the sake of all worlds. However, the following passage reveals his subtle transgression.

As in the Sūtra, the third assembly reconciles the provisional teachings. As the *Benye jing* (Sūtra of the Original Acts) states: "The stages prior to the seventh dwelling are of the nature of regression.
If one does not encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), then for one kalpa or even up to ten kalpas, one may regress from Bodhi."
As for the mind—just as in the cases of the Devaputra Śuddharaśmi, Prince Dharmamati, Śāriputra, and others—they desired to enter the seventh stage;
however, due to the conditions of encountering evil associates (pāpa-mitra) in the interim, they regressed and fell back into the unwholesome evils of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
This has been explained at length. Now, the explanation of this meaning is merely a provisional teaching (*upāya-vacana*); it is not an actual regression. Furthermore, because these bodhisattvas...
Below, the fourth [section] praises their actual practice, which is forever free from timidity; this establishes that the aforementioned sutra is provisional and not ultimate.
One should know that those who resolve their minds through understanding and practice are even more superior, because these bodhisattvas, from the time of their initial right faith onward, at...
As the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa was about to reach its completion, a profound understanding of the dharma of *tathatā* manifested before him.

Because his practice was free from signs and he realized that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, he practiced the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) in accordance with that realization.
Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance with it.
Because one knows that the nature of phenomena is without suffering and free from anger and affliction, one practices the *kṣānti-pāramitā* in accordance with it.
Because one knows that the nature of phenomena is devoid of the characteristics of body and mind and is free from indolence, one practices the *vīrya-pāramitā* in accordance with it.

Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally settled and its essence is without confusion, one practices the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) in accordance with this.
Because one knows that the essence of the nature of phenomena is luminous and free from ignorance, one practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in accordance with this.

Regarding the second point, the arousal of the mind through practice (*caryā-prasthāna-citta*): it is said that "because the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa is about to be completed, a profound understanding of suchness (*tathatā*) manifests.
This refers to the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), wherein one attains the emptiness of equality; thus, a profound understanding of suchness manifests.
This is because the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa prior to the [first] bhūmi is about to be fulfilled. This passage cites the stage of practice (*adhimukti-caryā*).

Regarding the generation of the bodhicitta that has been attained: it is subsequently stated that because one knows the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to be free from stinginess and greed, one practices in accordance with the perfections such as *dāna*.

This is because within the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-prayoga*), one attains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), thereby being able to cultivate the practice of the six perfections in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*.
This reveals the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) upon which the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is based.

Regarding the arousal of the mind through realization (*praveśa-cittotpāda*), there are two sections in the text: first, a general explanation of the arousal of the mind through realization as it pertains to all the stages (*bhūmi*);
second, a specific exposition of the virtues of fulfillment as they pertain to the ten stages.
Regarding the realization of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*): from the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*) up to the Ultimate Ground of the Bodhisattva, what is the realm that is realized?
It is called *tathatā* (suchness). While it is described as a "realm" based upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), for this realization there is no objective realm;
it is solely the wisdom of *tathatā*, which is termed the *dharmakāya*. In a single moment of thought, the bodhisattva is able to reach all ten directions without exception.

Throughout the worlds, he makes offerings to all Buddhas and requests them to turn the wheel of Dharma, solely for the purpose of guiding and benefiting sentient beings, rather than relying on mere words.
To those who are timid and weak, he may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment by transcending the stages;
to those who are indolent and lax, he may say, "I shall attain the Buddha-way after immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Thus, he is able to manifest [these various teachings].
Thus, through countless and inconceivable skillful means, the bodhisattvas' spiritual lineages and faculties are indeed equal;
their initial resolve is equal, and that which they realize is also equal, for there is no dharma by which one may surpass another, as all bodhisattvas pass through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
It is only according to the differences among sentient beings and worlds—based on what they see and hear, and their faculties, desires, and dispositions—that [distinctions appear].

Because they differ, it is shown that their modes of practice also have distinctions. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind, there are three subtle aspects of the mind.
What are these three? First is the true mind, because it is free from discrimination.

Second is the mind of skillful means, because it spontaneously and universally acts for the benefit of sentient beings. Third is the mind of karmic consciousness, which arises and ceases in a subtle manner.
Therefore, there are four sections in the beginning: first, the designation of the stage; second, the clarification of the meaning of realization (from "This bodhisattva...

onwards); third, the praise of virtues (from "The characteristics of generating the mind... onwards); and fourth, the manifestation of the characteristics. Within the second section, it says: "By relying on the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*)."

That which is called the "object" (ālambana) is the characteristic of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); it is the function of the perceiver. It is in relation to this perceiver that the object is designated.
This is because the realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) arising in these stages must depend upon the evolving consciousnesses to realize *tathatā*.

Therefore, in relation to its support, it is metaphorically termed an "object. However, with respect to the realized wisdom itself, there is neither subject nor object; thus, it is said that "one realizes."
There is no objective realm. Regarding the "true mind" mentioned in the fourth [section], this refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The "expedient mind" is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). The "karmic consciousness mind" is the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which is the basis for these two types of wisdom.

Speaking in terms of ultimate reality, there are also the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*); however, here we have briefly cited only the fundamental, subtle characteristics. Nevertheless...
This karmic consciousness is not the virtue of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

It is merely intended to show that when the two types of wisdom arise, there remains this subtle burden of arising and ceasing, which differs from the purely immaculate virtue of the Buddha-stage; therefore, it is described as the characteristic of generating the mind.
△ Below, the second section specifically elucidates the merit of fulfillment. This contains two parts: first, the direct manifestation of supreme virtues;
second, the removal of doubts through dialogue.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s merits are fully perfected, he manifests a body that is the highest and greatest in all worlds within the Akaniṣṭha realm.
That is to say, through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly exhausted; this is called the "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable activities capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the statement that "merits are perfected" at the beginning and middle [of the path], this refers to the perfection of causal practice in the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).
As for the manifestation of a vast and sublime body in the Akaniṣṭha realm, up to the designation "Omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) and so forth:
if one follows the specific gateway of the retributive fruits of the ten kings, the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is a king of the fourth dhyāna who resides in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
The Path refers to the *paranirmita-vaiśvāvana* body of the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*). As stated in the section on the "fruition of retribution" in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"A Bodhisattva of the ninth stage acts as a Great Brahmā King, presiding over two thousand worlds;
a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage acts as the Heavenly King Maheśvara, presiding over three thousand worlds. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "For example, it is like the *ālayavijñāna*..."
Instantly, one discerns that the body and the world of vessels are manifestations of one's own mind. The Reward Buddha (Saṃbhogakāya) Tathāgata is likewise:
in a single moment, he brings all realms of sentient beings to fulfillment and establishes them in the pure and wondrous palaces of the Ultimate Heaven (*Akaniṣṭha*), a place for practicing purity.
Furthermore, the following verse says: "In the Desire Realm and the Formless Realm, the Buddha does not attain Buddhahood; [he attains it] in the Form Realm..."
The gods of the middle and upper realms attain the Way while remaining within the midst of their desire.
(Separate Record) Now, explaining the intent of this sutra: if one discusses the meaning of the true *saṃbhogakāya*, it pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* and is not absent from any place.
Yet, to say that he attains Buddhahood specifically within the body of those gods is for the sake of...

The physical forms manifested by Bodhisattvas as transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) and enjoyment bodies (saṃbhogakāya) are not the actual retribution body (vipākakāya), which exists only in that [pure] heaven.
To clarify this meaning, the term "realm" (dhātu) is used. (The *Biejì* ends here.)

The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was in the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara in the Fourth Dhyāna, together with an immeasurable assembly of Great Brahmā Kings and unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Bodhisattvas."
This is the "Chapter on the Dharma-Door of the Mind-Ground" as taught by Vairocana Buddha in the Lotus Treasury World.
At that time, the body of Śākyamuni emitted rays of wisdom-light, extending from this Heavenly King’s Palace up to the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury World.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha lifted up the great assembly of this world and brought them to the palace of a hundred trillion purple-golden lights within the Lotus Treasury World.
There, Vairocana Buddha was seated upon a majestic throne of radiant light atop a hundred thousand lotuses.
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha and the entire multitude simultaneously paid their respects.
Homage to the Buddha Vairocana. At that time, the Buddha Vairocana was greatly rejoiced and said:
"O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively and contemplate this well for your practice. For a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have cultivated the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*) as my cause;
having first abandoned the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), I attained equal and perfect enlightenment and became Vairocana, dwelling in the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbhaloka*)."
In the ocean of worlds, its central terrace is surrounded by a thousand petals; each petal is one world, thus constituting a thousand worlds.
I manifest as a thousand Śākyamunis, each presiding over one of these thousand worlds.

Furthermore, within these thousand-petaled worlds, there are ten billion sets of four continents, where ten billion Bodhisattvas and Śākyamunis sit beneath ten billion bodhi trees, just as [in this world].
This thousand-petaled lotus Buddha is my transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies of these thousand Śākyamunis;
I am their source, named Vairocana. As the verse says: "I, Vairocana, now sit upon the lotus pedestal," and so forth, as explained at length.
These various passages may be understood by following this interpretation.
Question: Because space is limitless, worlds are limitless. Because worlds are limitless, sentient beings are limitless.
Because sentient beings are limitless, the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise limitless. Such a realm cannot be delimited;
it is difficult to know and difficult to understand. If ignorance is severed and no mental conceptions remain, how can one be said to "comprehend all" (sarvajña)?
[Question]: What is the knowledge of all modes? [Answer]: All objective realms are fundamentally the one mind, free from conceptualization and perception.

Because sentient beings falsely perceive objective realms, their minds possess limitations. Because they give rise to false conceptualizations that do not accord with the *dharmatā*, they are unable to decisively comprehend it.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas are free from views and perceptions; because their minds are true, there is nothing they do not pervade. This is precisely...
The nature of all phenomena is such that its own essence illuminates all deluded dharmas.
Possessing the function of great wisdom and immeasurable skillful means, it is able to reveal various meanings of the Dharma according to how each sentient being should attain understanding.

For this reason, it is named "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, he asked: "If all Buddhas possess spontaneous activity (*anābhoga-karman*) capable of manifesting benefit in all places..."

Regarding those who benefit sentient beings: among all sentient beings, there are none who do not obtain benefit—whether they see his body, behold his spiritual transformations, or hear his teachings.
Why is it that many in the world are unable to see him? The answer is: the Dharma-body of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is equal and pervasive in all places;
because it is free from intentional effort, it is said to be spontaneous (*svayambhū*). It simply accords with the minds of sentient beings.
The manifestation of the minds of sentient beings is like a mirror. If the mirror has impurities, forms and images do not appear;
likewise, if the minds of sentient beings have impurities, the Dharmakāya does not manifest.
The second section dispels doubts through two rounds of question and answer, thereby removing two types of uncertainty. Within the first answer, there are three parts:
first, establishing the principle; second, citing what is incorrect; and third, revealing what is correct.

Regarding the first, the statement that "all objective realms are fundamentally the one mind, free from conceptualization" establishes the principle. This means that although all objective realms are not limited by extremes, they...
It is not without limit, for it does not depart from the single mind. Because it is not without limit, it can be fully understood;
yet because it is not with limit, it is not an object of discursive thought. For this reason, it is said to be "free from conceptualization. Second, the phrase "not the middle" is raised.
Regarding the statement that "because sentient beings perceive objects through delusion, the mind has boundaries," this clarifies that there is something [to be known].
Because one sees, there is that which is not seen. The third [point] clarifies the Middle Way.
To say that "being free from the perception of seeing, there is nothing to which it does not pervade" means that because there is nothing seen, there is nothing not seen.

To say that "because the mind is true reality, it is the very nature of all phenomena" means that the Buddha-mind is free from conceptualization; its essence is the original source of the One Mind. Because it is free from deluded thoughts, it is so named.
The mind is reality. Because its essence is the One Mind, it constitutes the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Thus, the Buddha-mind is the substance of all deluded phenomena, and all deluded phenomena are the manifestations (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha-mind. These manifestations appear within its own substance, and the substance itself illuminates those manifestations.
To understand this clearly—what difficulty could there be? Therefore, it is said that the substance itself manifests and illuminates all things.
Regarding false phenomena: this refers to the reason why, because there is nothing seen, there is nothing not seen. Next, the second doubt is dispelled. In the response it says:
"If a mirror has impurities, forms and images do not appear; likewise, if the minds of sentient beings have impurities, the Dharma-body does not appear.
Here, the Dharma-body is like the original object, while the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) is like the reflected image. Now, based on this capacity...
Because it is the very nature of manifestation, it is said that the Dharmakāya does not manifest. As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding the profundity of manifestation:
"Due to [the world's] loss, the Honored One does not appear, just as the form of the moon does not appear in a broken vessel. The commentary explains:
Although the Buddhas do not manifest in the world, the world says that the bodies of the Buddhas are eternally abiding; why then do they not manifest? It is like [the moon in a broken vessel].
Just as water cannot remain in a broken vessel, and because the water does not remain, the moon that truly exists cannot manifest within that broken vessel,
so too for those sentient beings who lack the smooth continuity of *śamatha* and possess only a continuity of faults,
the Buddhas who truly exist do not manifest to them. Water is a metaphor for *śamatha*.
Because of its softness and smoothness. These two treatises explain the same meaning regarding the manifestation and non-manifestation of the Buddha;
however, there is a slight difference in their metaphors. In this present treatise, a mirror is used as a metaphor for that which does not manifest when it is defiled.

This is taught according to the capacities of sentient beings. When one perceives that the capacity for seeing the Buddha has matured, it is described as "stainless" (*vimala*). When there are still obstructions and the capacity has not yet matured, it is called "with stain" (*samala*).
This does not mean that the mere manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes being "with stain" and thus unable to see [the Buddha].

For instance, even though the afflictions were active within their minds, monks such as Sunakṣatra and Devadatta were nonetheless able to see the Buddha. In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, this is illustrated by the analogy of a vessel that has been broken.
Regarding the statement that one must possess *śamatha* in order to see the Buddha:

this clarifies that by maintaining the continuity of the cultivation of the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) from past lives, one is able to see the body of the Buddha in the present life.

It does not mean that one must rely on a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) in the present life to see the Buddha, for even with a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), one can still see the Buddha; as stated in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-śāstra*.

The commentary states: Furthermore, the sūtras teach that the various dhyānas are the spheres of practice (*caritaviṣaya*). Therefore, one who attains dhyāna is said to be "one who practices all practices well.
However, in this treatise, it is not necessary to have attained dhyāna in order to first resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment]. Why is this?
Because during the Buddha’s lifetime, immeasurable sentient beings also resolved upon the mind, yet they did not necessarily possess dhyāna.
